- Typical indications: node-positive colon cancer (stage III, FOLFOX/CAPOX), breast cancer (endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, trastuzumab), resected PDAC (mFOLFIRINOX, gemcitabine/capecitabine or gemcitabine for 6 months), melanoma and renal cell carcinoma (checkpoint inhibitors), *EGFR*-mutant lung cancer (osimertinib).
- Timing: usually start within 6–12 weeks after surgery.
- Biomarkers (e.g. ctDNA-based MRD) are being studied to select who needs adjuvant therapy.

German: adjuvante Therapie. Combined pre- and postoperative treatment is called perioperative therapy.

attrs.mnemonic: Adjuvant = 'aiding' after surgery has done the main job; the patient has 'no evidence of disease', so you are treating ghosts (micrometastases).

items.label_md: Palliative therapy and best supportive care
items.gloss_md: Treatment whose goal is to prolong life and relieve symptoms when cure is not possible; best supportive care means symptom-directed care without anticancer therapy.
items.body_md:
- Palliative anticancer therapy: chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy or radiotherapy given with non-curative intent, e.g. FOLFIRINOX for metastatic PDAC. Treatment continues as long as benefit outweighs toxicity.
- Best supportive care (BSC): pain control, nutrition, management of jaundice (stent), ascites, cachexia, depression; often the comparator arm in older trials.
- Palliative care as a discipline (Palliativmedizin) should be integrated early: Temel et al. (NEJM 2010) showed that early palliative care in metastatic NSCLC improved quality of life and was associated with longer survival.
- Palliative surgery and procedures: biliary or duodenal stenting, gastrojejunostomy, coeliac plexus neurolysis.

Treatment intent (curative vs palliative) is decided in the tumour board and determines how much toxicity is acceptable.

attrs.mnemonic: Pallium = cloak (Latin): palliative care cloaks the symptoms when the disease cannot be removed.

items.gloss_md: Perioperative therapy splits systemic treatment around surgery; total neoadjuvant therapy gives all planned chemotherapy (and radiotherapy) before surgery.
items.body_md:
- Perioperative: e.g. FLOT (5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel), 4 cycles before and 4 after gastrectomy for gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (FLOT4, Al-Batran et al., Lancet 2019).
- Total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT): rectal cancer, short-course radiotherapy plus chemotherapy (RAPIDO) or chemotherapy plus chemoradiation (PRODIGE 23) before surgery; high complete-response rates enable "watch and wait" organ preservation.
- In PDAC, total neoadjuvant approaches (e.g. 8 cycles of mFOLFIRINOX before resection) are used at many centres for borderline-resectable disease.

Advantages of TNT: higher compliance (postoperative chemotherapy is often not completed), earlier systemic control; disadvantage: possible overtreatment of patients who would have done well with surgery alone.

items.gloss_md: Induction therapy is an initial intensive treatment phase; conversion therapy aims to turn an initially unresectable tumour into a resectable one.
items.body_md:
- Induction chemotherapy: first phase of a planned sequence, e.g. FOLFIRINOX for 4–6 months in locally advanced PDAC before restaging and possible chemoradiation or surgery.
- Conversion surgery: resection after induction therapy in a patient initially classified as unresectable (locally advanced PDAC, colorectal liver metastases, HCC). Only a minority of locally advanced PDAC patients are converted, and selection relies on clinical response, CA19-9 decline and performance status, because CT poorly distinguishes fibrosis from viable tumour.
- Maintenance follows induction when the aim is disease control (see maintenance therapy).

The term "conversion" is also used in transplant medicine for switching immunosuppressants (e.g. calcineurin inhibitor to mTOR inhibitor), which is a different meaning.

items.gloss_md: Continued, usually less intensive treatment after induction therapy has achieved response or stable disease, to prolong disease control.
items.body_md:
Forms:
- Continuation maintenance: keep part of the induction regimen, e.g. stop oxaliplatin (cumulative neuropathy) and continue 5-FU/leucovorin after FOLFIRINOX induction in PDAC (PANOPTIMOX/PRODIGE 35 explored this "stop-and-go" approach), or bevacizumab + fluoropyrimidine in colorectal cancer.
- Switch maintenance: introduce a new drug, e.g. olaparib in germline *BRCA*-mutated metastatic PDAC after ≥16 weeks of platinum without progression (POLO), PARP inhibitors after platinum in ovarian cancer.

Endpoints are usually progression-free survival and quality of life; overall survival benefit is often not shown (as in POLO). Treatment breaks ("chemotherapy holidays") are an alternative.

items.gloss_md: The sequence of systemic treatments for advanced disease: first-line is the initial regimen, second-line follows progression or intolerance, and so on.
items.body_md:
- First-line (1L, Erstlinie): best available standard, chosen by performance status, comorbidity and biomarkers. Metastatic PDAC: FOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel.
- Second-line (2L): after progression, usually switching drug class (e.g. after gemcitabine-based therapy: liposomal irinotecan + 5-FU/LV or FOLFOX/OFF; after FOLFIRINOX: gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel).
- Later lines (3L+): fewer standard options; trials and molecularly matched therapy become important.

Changes in therapy due to toxicity without progression usually do not count as a new line; maintenance belongs to the line it follows. Line of therapy is a key trial eligibility criterion ("previously treated", "treatment-naive"). In PDAC, only about half of patients receive second-line therapy because of rapid clinical deterioration.

attrs.mnemonic: Lines are like a relay: each runner takes over when the previous one is exhausted (progression).

items.gloss_md: Surgical resection of cancer with the aim of complete removal with clear margins, adequate lymphadenectomy and minimal tumour-cell spillage.
items.body_md:
Principles:
- Resection with tumour-free margins (R0), en bloc removal of the tumour with involved adjacent structures.
- Systematic lymphadenectomy of the regional node stations for staging and local control (e.g. ≥12 nodes examined for colon and pancreas).
- "No-touch" technique and avoidance of tumour rupture.
- Staging laparoscopy when occult peritoneal disease is likely.
- Multidisciplinary planning: neoadjuvant therapy, reconstruction, adjuvant therapy.

Surgery is the only potentially curative treatment for most solid tumours, including PDAC. Outcomes depend strongly on hospital and surgeon volume, which is why many countries, including Germany (G-BA minimum volumes, "Mindestmengen", for complex pancreatic and oesophageal surgery), centralise complex cancer surgery. Morbidity is graded with Clavien–Dindo.

items.gloss_md: A state of limited metastatic spread (commonly up to 3–5 lesions) in which local treatment of all sites may prolong survival or even cure.
items.body_md:
Hellman and Weichselbaum proposed the concept in 1995 as an intermediate state between localised and widespread disease.

- Local therapies: metastasectomy (e.g. colorectal liver metastases, a well-established curative option), SBRT/SABR, thermal ablation.
- SABR-COMET (Palma et al., Lancet 2019), a randomised phase II trial across tumour types with up to 5 metastases, suggested improved overall survival with SABR added to standard care.
- ESTRO/EORTC classify oligometastatic disease into de novo, repeat and induced states.

In PDAC, resection of the primary with limited liver metastases is generally not recommended outside trials, although selected patients with isolated lung metastases or excellent response to chemotherapy are discussed in tumour boards.

items.gloss_md: Treatment with cytotoxic drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells, mainly by damaging DNA or disrupting cell division.
items.body_md:
- Main classes: alkylating agents, platinum compounds, antimetabolites, topoisomerase inhibitors, microtubule-targeting agents, cytotoxic antibiotics (anthracyclines).
- Dosing: by body surface area (mg/m²) or AUC (carboplatin), in cycles (e.g. every 14 or 21 days) that allow recovery of normal tissues.
- Combinations of drugs with different mechanisms and non-overlapping toxicities (e.g. FOLFIRINOX) increase efficacy.
- Typical toxicities from damage to fast-renewing tissues: myelosuppression (neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia), mucositis, diarrhoea, alopecia, nausea; plus drug-specific ones (oxaliplatin neuropathy, anthracycline cardiotoxicity, cisplatin nephrotoxicity).
- Settings: neoadjuvant, adjuvant, palliative, with radiotherapy (radiosensitising), high-dose with stem-cell rescue.

Chemotherapy remains the backbone of PDAC treatment in all stages. In everyday clinical talk, "Chemo" in German.

attrs.mnemonic: Chemo hits what divides fast: hair (alopecia), gut (mucositis, diarrhoea) and bone marrow (cytopenias) — 'hair, gut, marrow'.
attrs.anecdote: Chemotherapy grew out of chemical-warfare research: Goodman and Gilman treated a lymphoma patient with nitrogen mustard at Yale in 1942, and the 1943 Bari harbour disaster, where mustard-exposed sailors lost their white blood cells, reinforced the idea.

items.gloss_md: Cytotoxic drugs that mimic nucleotides or folates and block DNA and RNA synthesis, acting mainly in S phase.
items.body_md:
- Pyrimidine analogues: 5-fluorouracil (5-FU, inhibits thymidylate synthase; potentiated by leucovorin), capecitabine (oral 5-FU prodrug), S-1 and TAS-102 (trifluridine/tipiracil), gemcitabine (deoxycytidine analogue), cytarabine (leukaemia).
- Antifolates: methotrexate (DHFR inhibitor; leucovorin rescue), pemetrexed (lung cancer, mesothelioma).
- Purine analogues: 6-mercaptopurine, fludarabine, cladribine.

Toxicities: myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhoea, hand–foot syndrome (capecitabine), and pharmacogenetic risk (*DPYD* variants for fluoropyrimidines, *TPMT*/*NUDT15* for thiopurines). Gemcitabine and fluoropyrimidines are the two antimetabolite backbones of PDAC therapy. Because they act in S phase, schedules with prolonged exposure (continuous 5-FU infusion, weekly gemcitabine) are typical.

attrs.mnemonic: Antimetabolites are 'fake building blocks': the cell builds them into DNA or wastes enzymes on them.

items.gloss_md: Cytotoxic drugs (cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin) that form DNA crosslinks and adducts, blocking replication and transcription.
items.body_md:
- Cisplatin: lung, head and neck, bladder, germ-cell, cervical cancer; biliary cancer with gemcitabine. Toxicities: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, severe nausea, neuropathy.
- Carboplatin: dosed by AUC (Calvert formula); mainly myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia); ovarian and lung cancer.
- Oxaliplatin: diaminocyclohexane platinum; gastrointestinal cancers (FOLFOX, CAPOX, FOLFIRINOX); acute cold-induced dysaesthesia and cumulative sensory neuropathy.

DNA crosslinks are repaired by homologous recombination and the Fanconi anaemia pathway, so HR-deficient tumours (*BRCA1/2*, *PALB2*) are especially platinum-sensitive, the basis for preferring platinum-containing regimens and PARP-inhibitor maintenance in g*BRCA*-mutated PDAC.

attrs.anecdote: Barnett Rosenberg discovered cisplatin's effect by accident in 1965: electric current through platinum electrodes released platinum complexes that stopped E. coli from dividing.

items.gloss_md: Cytotoxic drugs that trap topoisomerase–DNA complexes, converting transient DNA breaks into permanent ones.
items.body_md:
- Topoisomerase I inhibitors (camptothecin derivatives): irinotecan (prodrug of SN-38; colorectal and pancreatic cancer in FOLFIRI, FOLFIRINOX), liposomal irinotecan (nal-IRI), topotecan; also the payloads of antibody–drug conjugates (deruxtecan in trastuzumab deruxtecan, SN-38 in sacituzumab govitecan).
- Topoisomerase II inhibitors: etoposide (small-cell lung cancer, NEC, germ-cell tumours) and anthracyclines (doxorubicin, epirubicin; also intercalate DNA; cumulative cardiotoxicity).

Topoisomerase II inhibitors are associated with therapy-related leukaemia with *KMT2A* (MLL) rearrangements. Topoisomerase I expression and *SLFN11* expression have been studied as predictive markers, without routine clinical use.

attrs.mnemonic: Topo I → Irinotecan (I with I); Topo II → etoposide and doxorubicin (double-strand breaks, two strands).

items.gloss_md: Cytotoxic drugs that disturb microtubule dynamics and arrest cells in mitosis.
items.body_md:
- Stabilisers (taxanes): paclitaxel, docetaxel, nab-paclitaxel (albumin-bound), cabazitaxel; prevent depolymerisation.
- Destabilisers: vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbine), eribulin; also the payloads monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) and maytansinoids (DM1) of antibody–drug conjugates.
- Main toxicities: peripheral sensory neuropathy (dose-limiting for vincristine and taxanes), neutropenia, hypersensitivity reactions (paclitaxel solvent Cremophor; avoided with nab-paclitaxel), alopecia.

In PDAC, nab-paclitaxel combined with gemcitabine is a first-line standard (MPACT trial). Docetaxel is part of FLOT for gastric cancer, and paclitaxel with carboplatin is used in oesophageal (CROSS), lung and ovarian cancer.

attrs.anecdote: Paclitaxel was isolated from the bark of the Pacific yew (Taxus brevifolia) in a US National Cancer Institute plant-screening programme; supplying early trials required stripping thousands of slow-growing trees until semi-synthesis from yew needles solved the problem.

items.gloss_md: Cytotoxic drugs that attach alkyl groups to DNA bases, causing crosslinks, strand breaks and mispairing.
items.body_md:
- Nitrogen mustards: cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide (haemorrhagic cystitis, prevented with mesna), melphalan, bendamustine, chlorambucil.
- Nitrosoureas: carmustine, lomustine (cross the blood–brain barrier).
- Triazenes: temozolomide (glioblastoma; efficacy depends on *MGMT* promoter methylation), dacarbazine.
- Others: busulfan; streptozocin (pancreatic NET).

Platinum compounds act similarly ("alkylating-like"). Long-term risks include infertility and secondary leukaemias. In pancreatic NETs, capecitabine plus temozolomide (CAPTEM) is a standard regimen. Mechanistically, O6-alkylguanine lesions are reversed by MGMT, which is why tumours with silenced *MGMT* respond better to temozolomide.

items.gloss_md: A deoxycytidine-analogue antimetabolite (2',2'-difluorodeoxycytidine) that is the backbone of many pancreatic and biliary cancer regimens.
items.body_md:
Mechanism: phosphorylated intracellularly (deoxycytidine kinase) to dFdCDP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, and dFdCTP, which is incorporated into DNA and causes masked chain termination. Uptake depends on nucleoside transporters (hENT1).

- PDAC: first-line monotherapy since Burris et al. (1997) showed better clinical benefit and modest survival gain over 5-FU; combined with nab-paclitaxel (MPACT); adjuvant alone (CONKO-001) or with capecitabine (ESPAC-4); in chemoradiation.
- Biliary tract cancer: gemcitabine + cisplatin + durvalumab or pembrolizumab.
- Others: NSCLC, bladder, ovarian, breast cancer.
- Dose: commonly 1000 mg/m² IV over 30 min, days 1, 8, 15 every 28 days.
- Toxicity: myelosuppression (especially thrombocytopenia), flu-like symptoms, elevated liver enzymes, rarely pneumonitis and haemolytic–uraemic syndrome. Generally well tolerated, so used for less fit patients.

attrs.mnemonic: Gem = 'the gem of pancreatic cancer' for 20 years (1997–2011), until FOLFIRINOX arrived.
attrs.anecdote: Gemcitabine was originally developed by Eli Lilly as an antiviral drug before its anticancer activity was recognised.

items.gloss_md: A fluoropyrimidine antimetabolite that inhibits thymidylate synthase; given with leucovorin (folinic acid) to enhance its effect.
items.body_md:
Mechanism: converted to FdUMP, which forms a ternary complex with thymidylate synthase (TS) and 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate (stabilised by leucovorin), blocking thymidine synthesis; FUTP is also incorporated into RNA.

- Regimens: FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, FOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX, FLOT, 5-FU/LV with liposomal irinotecan; with radiotherapy as a radiosensitiser.
- Administration: IV bolus and/or 46-hour continuous infusion via port and portable pump (mFOLFIRINOX drops the bolus).
- Toxicities: mucositis, diarrhoea, neutropenia (bolus), hand–foot syndrome (infusion), coronary vasospasm.
- Catabolised by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD); partial or complete DPD deficiency (*DPYD* variants) causes life-threatening toxicity, so pre-treatment testing is recommended in Europe.

Leucovorin is also called folinic acid (Folinsäure); levoleucovorin is the active isomer.

attrs.mnemonic: FOLF- = FOLinic acid + Fluorouracil: every 'FOLF' regimen contains 5-FU and leucovorin.
attrs.anecdote: 5-FU was rationally designed by Charles Heidelberger in 1957 after the observation that tumours take up uracil more avidly than normal tissue.

items.gloss_md: An oral prodrug of 5-fluorouracil, activated in three enzymatic steps, the last by thymidine phosphorylase that is enriched in tumour tissue.
items.body_md:
- Uses: adjuvant PDAC with gemcitabine (ESPAC-4), colorectal cancer (CAPOX/XELOX, monotherapy), breast cancer, biliary cancer adjuvant (BILCAP), pancreatic NET (CAPTEM), as a radiosensitiser in rectal cancer.
- Dosing: twice daily for 14 days of a 21-day cycle (schedules vary).
- Toxicities: hand–foot syndrome (palmar–plantar erythrodysaesthesia), diarrhoea, hyperbilirubinaemia; same *DPYD* risk as 5-FU.

Advantages: oral, avoids a port and infusion pump, and can replace infusional 5-FU in many regimens (e.g. CAPOX instead of FOLFOX). Disadvantages: adherence and dose adjustments rest with the patient, and renal impairment increases toxicity. Trade name: Xeloda.

attrs.mnemonic: Cape-'site'-abine: the final activation step happens at the tumour site (thymidine phosphorylase).

items.gloss_md: A third-generation platinum compound used mainly in gastrointestinal cancers, characterised by cold-induced acute neuropathy and cumulative sensory neuropathy.
items.body_md:
- Mechanism: platinum–DNA adducts and crosslinks; its bulky diaminocyclohexane ligand makes adducts less recognisable by mismatch repair, giving activity in colorectal cancer where cisplatin is weak.
- Regimens: FOLFOX, CAPOX, FLOT, FOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX, OFF (second-line PDAC).
- Toxicities: acute neurotoxicity (cold-triggered paraesthesias, laryngopharyngeal dysaesthesia; patients avoid cold drinks during infusion), cumulative dose-dependent sensory neuropathy (often limiting after about 6 months, may persist), neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hypersensitivity reactions.

"Stop-and-go" strategies (pausing oxaliplatin while continuing 5-FU) reduce neuropathy. HR-deficient PDACs respond particularly well to oxaliplatin-containing regimens.

attrs.mnemonic: Oxali-'chilly'-platin: the cold-induced neuropathy — no ice cream on infusion day.

items.gloss_md: A topoisomerase I inhibitor prodrug converted to SN-38; liposomal irinotecan (nal-IRI) is a nanoliposomal formulation used in pancreatic cancer.
items.body_md:
- Activation by carboxylesterases to SN-38; inactivation by glucuronidation via UGT1A1. Patients homozygous for *UGT1A1*\*28 (Gilbert syndrome genotype) have higher SN-38 exposure and more neutropenia, so dose reduction is considered.
- Toxicity: early cholinergic syndrome (sweating, cramps, diarrhoea within 24 h; treated with atropine), late diarrhoea (high-dose loperamide), neutropenia, alopecia.
- Regimens: FOLFIRI (colorectal), FOLFIRINOX (PDAC).
- Liposomal irinotecan (nal-IRI, Onivyde): longer circulation and tumour accumulation; with 5-FU/LV in second-line PDAC after gemcitabine (NAPOLI-1) and in first-line NALIRIFOX (NAPOLI-3).

attrs.mnemonic: Irinotecan → 'diarrhoea-notecan': early (cholinergic → atropine) and late (→ loperamide) diarrhoea.

items.gloss_md: Nanoparticle albumin-bound paclitaxel, a solvent-free taxane formulation used with gemcitabine in pancreatic cancer.
items.body_md:
- Formulation: paclitaxel bound to albumin (~130 nm particles), avoiding the Cremophor solvent of conventional paclitaxel, so no premedication against hypersensitivity is required and higher doses can be given.
- It was hypothesised to accumulate in tumours via albumin-binding proteins (SPARC) and to deplete stroma, but SPARC did not prove predictive.
- PDAC: gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² + nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m² on days 1, 8, 15 every 28 days (MPACT); also used in neoadjuvant and second-line settings (after FOLFIRINOX).
- Also approved for breast and non-small-cell lung cancer.
- Toxicities: neutropenia, peripheral neuropathy, fatigue, alopecia.

Trade name: Abraxane.

attrs.mnemonic: nab = nanoparticle albumin-bound: albumin is the 'taxi' for the taxane.

items.gloss_md: Reduced activity of the enzyme that degrades 5-FU, usually due to *DPYD* variants, which causes severe or fatal fluoropyrimidine toxicity unless the dose is reduced.
items.body_md:
DPD (encoded by *DPYD*) degrades about 80% of administered 5-FU. Partial deficiency affects a few percent of Europeans; complete deficiency is rare.

- Key variants: *DPYD*\*2A (c.1905+1G>A), c.1679T>G (\*13), c.2846A>T and c.1236G>A (HapB3).
- Gene activity score (0–2) guides dosing (e.g. 50% starting dose at activity score 1; avoid fluoropyrimidines at 0).
- Since 2020, the European Medicines Agency recommends testing before starting 5-FU, capecitabine or tegafur, by genotyping or phenotyping (plasma uracil concentration).
- Germany: genotyping of the four variants is standard before FOLFIRINOX, FOLFOX or capecitabine.

Related pharmacogenetics: *UGT1A1*\*28 for irinotecan.

items.label_md: Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE)
items.gloss_md: The US National Cancer Institute's standard dictionary and 1–5 severity scale for adverse events in cancer treatment.
items.body_md:
Grades (general scheme, version 5.0):
- Grade 1: mild; asymptomatic or mild symptoms, intervention not indicated.
- Grade 2: moderate; minimal, local or non-invasive intervention, limiting instrumental activities of daily living.
- Grade 3: severe or medically significant but not immediately life-threatening; hospitalisation indicated; limiting self-care.
- Grade 4: life-threatening consequences; urgent intervention indicated.
- Grade 5: death related to the adverse event.

Each event term has specific definitions (e.g. neutropenia grade 4: neutrophils <500/µL). Dose modifications in protocols and trials ("hold for grade ≥3") rely on CTCAE, and trial publications report "grade ≥3 adverse events". Immune-related adverse events and surgical complications use other systems in parallel (Clavien–Dindo for surgery).

attrs.mnemonic: CTCAE grade = 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3 severe, 4 life-threatening, 5 death — like Clavien–Dindo, 5 is always death.

items.gloss_md: Fever in a patient with a low neutrophil count after chemotherapy, an oncological emergency requiring immediate empirical antibiotics.
items.body_md:
- Definition (common, IDSA/ESMO-like): absolute neutrophil count <500/µL (or expected to fall below 500/µL) and a single oral temperature ≥38.3 °C or ≥38.0 °C sustained over one hour.
- Management: blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam) within one hour; risk stratification (MASCC score) for outpatient management of low-risk patients.
- Prevention: granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF: filgrastim, pegfilgrastim) as primary prophylaxis when the regimen's febrile neutropenia risk is ≥20% (or 10–20% with risk factors), e.g. often with FOLFIRINOX.

Neutrophil nadir usually occurs 7–14 days after chemotherapy.

items.gloss_md: Treatment with ionising radiation that kills tumour cells mainly by causing DNA double-strand breaks, delivered externally or internally.
items.body_md:
- Dose unit: gray (Gy, 1 J/kg). Conventional fractionation 1.8–2 Gy per day, 5 days a week; hypofractionation uses fewer, larger fractions; the biologically effective dose (BED, linear–quadratic model with α/β ratio) compares schedules.
- Techniques: 3D-conformal, intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), volumetric-modulated arc therapy (VMAT), image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT), stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT/SABR), particle therapy (protons, carbon ions, e.g. at the Heidelberg Ion-Beam Therapy Center).
- Internal: brachytherapy, radionuclide therapy (¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE, ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA, ⁹⁰Y radioembolisation of liver tumours).
- Intent: curative (alone or with chemotherapy), neoadjuvant/adjuvant, palliative (pain from bone metastases, bleeding, compression).

Targets: GTV (gross tumour), CTV (+ microscopic spread), PTV (+ set-up margin). In PDAC, radiotherapy has a limited, debated role: chemoradiation after induction chemotherapy did not prolong survival in LAP07, but it is used for local control, pain and in some neoadjuvant protocols (PREOPANC).

attrs.mnemonic: GTV ⊂ CTV ⊂ PTV: Gross (see it), Clinical (suspect it), Planning (miss it otherwise).
attrs.anecdote: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in Würzburg in 1895, and within a year X-rays were being used to treat cancer; he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

items.gloss_md: Highly precise radiotherapy delivering very high doses in a few fractions (usually 1–8) to a small target with steep dose fall-off.
items.body_md:
Also called stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR). Requires precise immobilisation, motion management (4D-CT, breath-hold, gating, fiducial markers) and image guidance; MR-linac systems allow daily adaptive planning, useful for pancreatic tumours next to the bowel.

- Established uses: early-stage inoperable lung cancer, oligometastases (lung, liver, bone, brain = stereotactic radiosurgery), HCC (as an alternative to ablation), spinal metastases.
- PDAC: used for locally advanced disease and in some neoadjuvant protocols for local control and pain; dose is limited by the adjacent duodenum and stomach; survival benefit unproven (the SBRT arm of Alliance A021501 was not superior).
- Radiobiology: high doses per fraction cause vascular damage and may enhance immunogenic cell death (abscopal effect, rare).

items.gloss_md: Concurrent radiotherapy and chemotherapy in which the drug (often a fluoropyrimidine, gemcitabine or platinum) sensitises tumour cells to radiation.
items.body_md:
- Standard of care in: rectal cancer (5-FU or capecitabine-based, neoadjuvant), oesophageal cancer (CROSS: carboplatin/paclitaxel), anal cancer (mitomycin/5-FU, curative without surgery), head and neck, cervical cancer, glioblastoma (temozolomide), limited-stage SCLC.
- PDAC: no proven survival benefit after induction chemotherapy in locally advanced disease (LAP07), but neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiation improved long-term survival in the Dutch PREOPANC trial; usage varies between countries (more common in the US and Netherlands than Germany).
- German: Radiochemotherapie (RCT or RCHT).

items.gloss_md: Drugs that act on specific molecules driving a tumour, typically an altered oncogenic protein or pathway, selected by a biomarker.
items.body_md:
Main modalities:
- Small-molecule inhibitors (suffix -ib), mostly kinase inhibitors (-tinib): imatinib (BCR::ABL1), osimertinib (*EGFR*), alectinib (*ALK*), dabrafenib + trametinib (*BRAF* V600E + MEK), sotorasib and adagrasib (*KRAS* G12C), olaparib (PARP).
- Monoclonal antibodies (suffix -mab): trastuzumab (HER2), cetuximab (EGFR), bevacizumab (VEGF).
- Antibody–drug conjugates (antibody + cytotoxic payload).

Principles: a predictive biomarker selects patients (companion diagnostic); responses can be dramatic in oncogene-addicted tumours but resistance usually develops (secondary target mutations, bypass pathways, lineage switching). Toxicities are mechanism-based (rash and diarrhoea with EGFR inhibitors, hypertension with VEGF inhibitors).

In PDAC, targeted therapy matters for small subgroups: g*BRCA* (olaparib maintenance), *KRAS* G12C, *KRAS*-wild-type tumours with fusions (*NTRK*, *NRG1*, *ALK*, *RET*) or *BRAF* alterations, and HER2 amplification; RAS(ON) inhibitors aim to broaden this to most patients. Erlotinib + gemcitabine (PA.3, 2007) gave only a marginal benefit and is obsolete.

attrs.mnemonic: -mab = monoclonal antibody (big, injected, outside the cell); -nib = inhibitor (small, oral, inside the cell).
attrs.anecdote: Imatinib (Glivec, approved 2001) turned chronic myeloid leukaemia from a fatal disease into a chronic condition and appeared on the cover of TIME magazine in May 2001, pictured as ammunition in the war against cancer.

items.gloss_md: Orally available small molecules that block the catalytic activity of protein kinases, typically by competing with ATP.
items.body_md:
- Classes: tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs; imatinib, erlotinib, osimertinib, lorlatinib), serine/threonine kinase inhibitors (vemurafenib, trametinib), CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib), multikinase inhibitors (sorafenib, lenvatinib, regorafenib, cabozantinib; important for HCC).
- Binding modes: type I (active conformation), type II (inactive DFG-out, imatinib), allosteric (MEK inhibitors), covalent (osimertinib, KRAS G12C inhibitors bind cysteine).
- Resistance: gatekeeper mutations (*EGFR* T790M, *BCR*::*ABL1* T315I), bypass signalling, amplification, histological transformation; generations of drugs are developed to overcome them.
- Practical issues: CYP3A4 interactions (relevant with tacrolimus in transplant patients), oral adherence, class toxicities.

items.gloss_md: Therapeutic antibodies that bind tumour antigens, growth-factor receptors, ligands or immune checkpoints to kill tumour cells or modulate signalling and immunity.
items.body_md:
- Mechanisms: receptor blockade (cetuximab, panitumumab: EGFR; trastuzumab: HER2), ligand neutralisation (bevacizumab: VEGF-A), immune effector functions (ADCC, ADCP, complement; rituximab: CD20), immune checkpoint blockade (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, ipilimumab), delivery of payloads (ADCs) and T-cell redirection (bispecifics).
- Classic INN suffixes: -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab fully human, -omab murine. Since 2022, new antibodies receive the stems -tug, -bart, -mig and -ment instead of -mab.
- Anti-EGFR antibodies work in colorectal cancer only when *KRAS* and *NRAS* are wild-type, the classic example of a negative predictive biomarker.

Antibodies are given IV or SC, have long half-lives (days to weeks) and do not cross the blood–brain barrier well.

attrs.mnemonic: -ximab chimeric (xi = 'mixed'), -zumab humanised (zu = 'human-ish'), -umab fully human (u = 'human').
attrs.anecdote: Köhler and Milstein invented the hybridoma technique for monoclonal antibodies in 1975 and deliberately did not patent it; they shared the 1984 Nobel Prize with Niels Jerne.

items.gloss_md: Antibodies that block inhibitory immune receptors or their ligands (PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4, LAG-3) to release T cells from suppression so they attack the tumour.
items.body_md:
- Targets and drugs: PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab), PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab), CTLA-4 (ipilimumab, tremelimumab), LAG-3 (relatlimab with nivolumab).
- Approved across many cancers: melanoma, NSCLC, renal, bladder, head and neck, HCC, biliary tract cancer, MSI-H/dMMR tumours of any site, and others.
- Biomarkers: PD-L1 expression (TPS, CPS), MSI-H/dMMR, TMB; none is perfect.
- Response pattern: a minority respond, but responses can be very durable ("tail of the curve"); pseudoprogression is possible.
- Toxicity: immune-related adverse events affecting any organ.

PDAC is largely resistant (cold tumour) except for the ~1% MSI-H/dMMR cases; combinations with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, CD40 agonists or vaccines are being tested.

attrs.mnemonic: Checkpoint inhibitors 'release the brakes' of T cells — they do not press the accelerator.
attrs.anecdote: James Allison (CTLA-4) and Tasuku Honjo (PD-1) received the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering cancer therapy by inhibition of negative immune regulation; Honjo's lab had originally identified PD-1 in 1992 while studying programmed cell death, hence the name 'programmed death-1'.

items.gloss_md: Checkpoint-inhibitor antibodies that bind the T-cell receptor PD-1 and block its interaction with PD-L1 and PD-L2.
items.body_md:
- Drugs: nivolumab (Opdivo, BMS), pembrolizumab (Keytruda, MSD), cemiplimab, dostarlimab, tislelizumab, toripalimab; both nivolumab and pembrolizumab were first approved in 2014 for melanoma.
- Mechanism: PD-1 on exhausted, chronically stimulated T cells dampens TCR/CD28 signalling when engaged by PD-L1 on tumour or myeloid cells; blockade reinvigorates T cells, especially progenitor-exhausted TCF1⁺ CD8 cells.
- Biomarkers: PD-L1 IHC (TPS in NSCLC, CPS in gastric/oesophageal/head-and-neck, with assay-specific antibodies such as 22C3), MSI-H/dMMR, TMB-high.
- Key indications: melanoma, NSCLC, renal cell carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, urothelial, head and neck, gastric and oesophageal cancers, MSI-H colorectal and any dMMR tumour, adjuvant settings.
- In biliary tract cancer, pembrolizumab + gemcitabine/cisplatin is a first-line standard (KEYNOTE-966).

Pembrolizumab became widely known when it cured metastatic melanoma with brain metastases in former US president Jimmy Carter (2015).

attrs.mnemonic: 'PD-1 sits on the T cell (1 = one soldier), PD-L1 is the Ligand on the tumour': anti-PD-1 covers the soldier's eyes so he can't see the 'calm down' signal.
attrs.anecdote: Former US president Jimmy Carter announced in December 2015 that his metastatic melanoma with brain metastases had disappeared after radiotherapy and pembrolizumab; he lived until December 2024, aged 100.

items.gloss_md: Checkpoint-inhibitor antibodies that bind PD-L1 on tumour and immune cells and block its interaction with PD-1 (and CD80).
items.body_md:
- Atezolizumab (Tecentriq, Roche): first anti-PD-L1 approval (2016, urothelial cancer); with bevacizumab first-line in HCC (IMbrave150), NSCLC, SCLC.
- Durvalumab (Imfinzi, AstraZeneca): consolidation after chemoradiation in stage III NSCLC (PACIFIC); with gemcitabine/cisplatin first-line in biliary tract cancer (TOPAZ-1); with tremelimumab in HCC (STRIDE regimen, HIMALAYA).
- Avelumab (Bavencio): Merkel cell carcinoma, maintenance in urothelial cancer.

Differences to anti-PD-1: PD-L2–PD-1 interactions remain possible, and anti-PD-L1 also blocks PD-L1–CD80 binding; clinically, efficacy and toxicity are broadly similar, with somewhat fewer pneumonitis events in some comparisons. PD-L1 IHC uses assay-specific antibodies (SP263, SP142, 22C3, 28-8).

attrs.mnemonic: Anti-PD-L1 blocks the Ligand on the tumour side; anti-PD-1 blocks the receptor on the T-cell side — same handshake, different hand.

items.gloss_md: Checkpoint-inhibitor antibodies that block CTLA-4, enhancing T-cell priming in lymph nodes and depleting intratumoural regulatory T cells.
items.body_md:
- Mechanism: CTLA-4 on activated T cells and Tregs outcompetes CD28 for CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells; blocking it lowers the activation threshold during priming. Some antibodies also deplete CTLA-4-high Tregs via Fc-mediated mechanisms.
- Ipilimumab (Yervoy, BMS): the first checkpoint inhibitor, approved 2011 for metastatic melanoma (first drug to prolong survival in that disease); combined with nivolumab in melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, NSCLC, MSI-H colorectal cancer, HCC.
- Tremelimumab: with durvalumab in HCC (single priming dose, STRIDE) and NSCLC.
- Toxicity is higher than with PD-1 blockade, especially colitis and hypophysitis; with ipilimumab + nivolumab, more than half of melanoma patients have grade 3–4 events.

attrs.mnemonic: CTLA-4 acts early in the lymph node (priming, 'the start line'), PD-1 later in the tumour (effector phase, 'the finish line').
attrs.anecdote: James Allison showed in 1996 that CTLA-4 blockade made mouse tumours regress; pharmaceutical companies were initially uninterested, and it took 15 years until ipilimumab's approval in 2011.

items.gloss_md: Autoimmune-like inflammatory side effects of immune-checkpoint inhibitors that can affect any organ.
items.body_md:
- Frequent: dermatitis and pruritus, colitis and diarrhoea, hepatitis, thyroiditis (hypo- or hyperthyroidism), pneumonitis, arthritis.
- Endocrine: hypophysitis (typical for anti-CTLA-4), primary adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune diabetes with ketoacidosis; usually irreversible and needing lifelong hormone replacement.
- Rare but dangerous: myocarditis (often with myositis and myasthenia, high mortality), encephalitis, haematological irAEs.
- Timing: usually within the first months but can occur late, even after stopping treatment.
- Management by CTCAE grade (ESMO/ASCO guidelines): grade 1 continue with monitoring; grade 2 hold and consider corticosteroids; grade 3–4 high-dose corticosteroids (e.g. 1–2 mg/kg prednisolone), stop the ICI, add infliximab or vedolizumab (colitis) or mycophenolate (hepatitis) if steroid-refractory.

In transplant recipients, checkpoint inhibitors carry a high risk of graft rejection.

attrs.mnemonic: '-itis everywhere': colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, dermatitis, myocarditis.

items.gloss_md: Adoptive cell therapy with the patient's T cells genetically engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that recognises a tumour surface antigen independently of MHC.
items.body_md:
- CAR structure: an antibody-derived single-chain variable fragment (scFv), hinge and transmembrane domain, a costimulatory domain (CD28 or 4-1BB) and the CD3ζ signalling domain ("second-generation CAR").
- Process: leukapheresis → lentiviral/retroviral transduction and expansion (2–4 weeks) → lymphodepleting chemotherapy (fludarabine/cyclophosphamide) → single infusion.
- Approved targets: CD19 (B-ALL, large B-cell lymphoma, follicular and mantle-cell lymphoma; tisagenlecleucel was first approved in 2017, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel) and BCMA (multiple myeloma; idecabtagene vicleucel, ciltacabtagene autoleucel).
- Toxicities: cytokine release syndrome (CRS, treated with tocilizumab), immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS, corticosteroids), B-cell aplasia, cytopenias, rare secondary T-cell malignancies.

Solid tumours remain difficult (antigen heterogeneity, hostile TME, trafficking); targets under investigation in PDAC include claudin 18.2, mesothelin and CEA.

attrs.mnemonic: CAR = Chimeric Antigen Receptor: an antibody 'steering wheel' welded onto a T-cell 'engine'.
attrs.anecdote: Emily Whitehead, a 6-year-old with relapsed ALL, was the first child to receive CD19 CAR-T cells (2012, Philadelphia); she nearly died from cytokine release syndrome, was rescued with tocilizumab, and remained in remission for over a decade.

items.gloss_md: Engineered antibodies that bind a tumour antigen with one arm and CD3 on T cells with the other, bringing T cells into contact with tumour cells regardless of their TCR specificity.
items.body_md:
- Blinatumomab (CD19 × CD3, BiTE format): B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; continuous infusion because of its short half-life.
- Lymphoma and myeloma: glofitamab, epcoritamab, mosunetuzumab (CD20 × CD3); teclistamab, elranatamab (BCMA × CD3); talquetamab (GPRC5D × CD3).
- Solid tumours: tebentafusp (gp100–HLA-A*02:01 × CD3, an ImmTAC, uveal melanoma, first to prolong survival in that disease), tarlatamab (DLL3 × CD3, small-cell lung cancer, 2024).

Off-the-shelf alternative to CAR-T cells; shared toxicities are cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity, usually milder, managed by step-up dosing.

items.gloss_md: Monoclonal antibodies linked chemically to a potent cytotoxic payload, delivering chemotherapy selectively to cells that express the target antigen.
items.body_md:
- Components: antibody (target selection), linker (cleavable or non-cleavable), payload (microtubule inhibitors MMAE, DM1; topoisomerase I inhibitors deruxtecan, SN-38), and drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR, ~2–8).
- Bystander effect: membrane-permeable payloads released from cleavable linkers kill neighbouring antigen-negative cells, which helps in heterogeneous tumours.
- Examples: trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1, HER2), trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd, HER2; active even in HER2-low breast cancer and tumour-agnostic FDA approval in 2024 for HER2 IHC 3+ solid tumours), sacituzumab govitecan (Trop-2), enfortumab vedotin (Nectin-4, urothelial cancer), brentuximab vedotin (CD30), mirvetuximab soravtansine (folate receptor α).
- Toxicities follow payload and target: interstitial lung disease (T-DXd), neuropathy (MMAE), ocular toxicity, neutropenia.

ADCs against targets such as claudin 18.2, mesothelin and Trop-2 are being explored in PDAC.

attrs.mnemonic: ADC = 'Trojan horse': the antibody is the horse, the payload the soldiers inside.

items.gloss_md: Vaccines that prevent virus-associated cancers (preventive) or that stimulate an immune response against antigens of an existing tumour (therapeutic).
items.body_md:
- Preventive: HPV vaccine (cervical, anal, oropharyngeal cancer), hepatitis B vaccine (HCC); among the most effective cancer-prevention measures.
- Therapeutic: sipuleucel-T (autologous dendritic-cell product, prostate cancer, 2010); BCG instillation for bladder cancer (non-specific immunotherapy).
- Personalised neoantigen vaccines (mRNA, peptides, dendritic cells): mRNA-4157/V940 plus pembrolizumab reduced recurrence after melanoma resection in a randomised phase IIb trial (KEYNOTE-942).
- PDAC: in a phase I trial (Rojas et al., Nature 2023) the individualised mRNA neoantigen vaccine autogene cevumeran (BioNTech/Genentech), given after resection with atezolizumab and mFOLFIRINOX, induced T-cell responses in half of the patients, and responders had delayed recurrence; a randomised phase II trial followed. Off-the-shelf *KRAS*-targeted vaccines (e.g. ELI-002) are also being tested.

Historically, many therapeutic vaccines (e.g. GVAX, telomerase peptide GV1001 in PDAC) failed in phase III.

attrs.anecdote: Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci founded BioNTech in Mainz in 2008 to develop individualised mRNA cancer vaccines; the mRNA platform they built for cancer was then used for the COVID-19 vaccine in 2020.

items.gloss_md: Small-molecule inhibitors of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase that are synthetically lethal with homologous recombination deficiency, e.g. in *BRCA1/2*-mutated tumours.
items.body_md:
- Drugs: olaparib (first approved 2014, ovarian cancer), niraparib, rucaparib, talazoparib.
- Mechanism: catalytic inhibition plus "PARP trapping" on single-strand breaks; the trapped complexes collapse replication forks into double-strand breaks that HR-deficient cells cannot repair.
- Indications: ovarian cancer (maintenance after platinum), breast cancer (g*BRCA*, including adjuvant olaparib in OlympiA), prostate cancer (HRR-mutated), and PDAC (olaparib maintenance in g*BRCA*-mutated metastatic disease after platinum, POLO).
- Platinum sensitivity predicts PARP-inhibitor benefit because both depend on HR deficiency.
- Resistance: *BRCA* reversion mutations, loss of 53BP1/shieldin, drug efflux.
- Toxicities: anaemia, fatigue, nausea, thrombocytopenia, rarely MDS/AML.

attrs.mnemonic: PARP-i 'parks' PARP on the DNA (trapping) — a parked car on a one-lane road (replication fork) causes the crash that BRCA-deficient cells cannot clear.

items.gloss_md: A regular meeting in which specialists from all relevant disciplines jointly review individual cancer cases and agree on a treatment recommendation.
items.body_md:
- Participants: surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology, radiology, pathology, gastroenterology, nuclear medicine, palliative care, often psycho-oncology, study nurses and, for molecular questions, human genetics and bioinformatics.
- Typical decisions: resectability, neoadjuvant vs upfront surgery, adjuvant therapy, palliative treatment, inclusion in clinical trials.
- Timing: pre-therapeutic (after staging) and post-operative (after histology), plus at recurrence or progression.
- In Germany, DKG-certified cancer centres must present all primary cases; the recommendation is documented in a structured protocol ("Tumorkonferenzbeschluss") and is the basis for billing and cancer-registry reporting.

For pancreatic cancer, resectability assessment in a high-volume pancreatic tumour board with dedicated radiologists is strongly recommended because CT interpretation of vessel contact is decisive.

attrs.mnemonic: The tumour board is the 'round table' of oncology: no single specialty decides alone.

items.gloss_md: A tumour board that interprets comprehensive molecular profiling of a patient's tumour and recommends molecularly targeted therapies or trials.
items.body_md:
- Inputs: NGS panel, whole-exome/genome and RNA sequencing, IHC (HER2, MMR, PD-L1), germline findings, previous therapies.
- Participants: oncologists, molecular pathologists, human geneticists, bioinformaticians, biologists, pharmacists.
- Output: variants ranked by an evidence scale (ESCAT, OncoKB levels or the German NCT/DKTK evidence levels), recommended drugs (often off-label, needing insurance approval), trial options, germline-referral advice.
- Germany: offered at Comprehensive Cancer Centres and the NCT sites; the national network DNPM (Deutsches Netzwerk für Personalisierte Medizin) and the genome-sequencing model project under §64e SGB V (since 2024) standardise access and data sharing.

Bioinformaticians typically run the variant-calling pipelines, annotate variants and present the data, so this is the tumour board where the learner's work is most visible.

attrs.mnemonic: Tumour board asks 'which treatment?', MTB asks 'which target?'.

items.gloss_md: Selecting cancer treatment based on the molecular characteristics of the individual tumour (and patient), rather than tumour site and histology alone.
items.body_md:
Components:
- Molecular profiling: targeted NGS panels (e.g. FoundationOne CDx, TruSight Oncology 500), WES/WGS, RNA-seq for fusions and expression, IHC, liquid biopsy.
- Interpretation: driver vs passenger, actionability tiers (ESCAT, OncoKB, AMP/ASCO/CAP), germline implications.
- Delivery: molecular tumour boards, companion diagnostics, biomarker-driven trials (basket trials test one drug across tumour types with the same alteration; umbrella trials test several drugs within one tumour type).

Evidence: dramatic benefit in oncogene-addicted subgroups (*EGFR*, *ALK*, *BRAF*, *NTRK*), but in unselected populations only a minority of patients (often 10–25%) receive a matched therapy. In PDAC, about a quarter of tumours carry a potentially actionable alteration (Know Your Tumor programme, Pishvaian et al. 2020), and patients who received matched therapy lived longer in that non-randomised analysis.

attrs.mnemonic: Basket = one drug, many tumour types in the basket; umbrella = one tumour type, many drugs under the umbrella.

items.label_md: ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT)
items.gloss_md: ESMO's tiered ranking of genomic alterations by the strength of clinical evidence that matching them to a drug improves outcome.
items.body_md:
Published by Mateo et al. (Annals of Oncology 2018).
- Tier I: ready for routine use. I-A prospective randomised evidence; I-B prospective non-randomised trials; I-C basket trials across tumour types.
- Tier II: investigational, likely to define a patient population that benefits but more data needed (II-A retrospective, II-B prospective without clear benefit).
- Tier III: clinical benefit shown in another tumour type or for a similar alteration (hypothetical).
- Tier IV: preclinical evidence only.
- Tier V: evidence for co-targeting approaches.
- Tier X: lack of evidence for actionability.

Example in PDAC: g*BRCA1/2* for olaparib is tier I-A; MSI-H/dMMR for checkpoint inhibitors and *NTRK* fusions are tier I-C. Similar scales: OncoKB levels 1–4/R1–R2 and AMP/ASCO/CAP tiers I–IV.

items.gloss_md: A diagnostic test that is required for the safe and effective use of a specific drug, typically to identify the biomarker-positive patients for whom it is approved.
items.body_md:
Examples:
- HER2 IHC/ISH for trastuzumab and trastuzumab deruxtecan.
- PD-L1 IHC 22C3 (TPS/CPS) for pembrolizumab in several indications.
- *KRAS*/*NRAS* (*RAS*) testing before anti-EGFR antibodies in colorectal cancer.
- Germline *BRCA* testing (e.g. BRACAnalysis CDx) for olaparib, including in PDAC.
- *EGFR*, *ALK*, *ROS1* testing in NSCLC.

A complementary diagnostic informs about benefit but is not mandatory for prescribing. In the EU, companion diagnostics are regulated by the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) with consultation of the drug regulator. In-house (lab-developed) tests at university pathology departments must show equivalence.

items.gloss_md: Regulatory approval of a drug for any solid tumour carrying a specific biomarker, regardless of the organ of origin.
items.body_md:
FDA milestones:
- 2017 pembrolizumab for MSI-H/dMMR solid tumours (the first).
- 2018 larotrectinib and 2019 entrectinib for *NTRK* fusions (also EMA).
- 2020 pembrolizumab for TMB-high (≥10 mut/Mb).
- 2021 dostarlimab for dMMR solid tumours.
- 2022 dabrafenib + trametinib for *BRAF* V600E; selpercatinib for *RET* fusions.
- 2024 trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2 IHC 3+ solid tumours.

These approvals are based on basket trials with response rates and response duration rather than randomised survival data. They are particularly relevant for rare subsets of PDAC (dMMR ~1%, *NTRK*/*RET* fusions and *BRAF* V600E in *KRAS*-wild-type tumours), which is why comprehensive molecular profiling is recommended in advanced PDAC. EMA approvals are fewer and sometimes narrower than the FDA's.

items.gloss_md: The stepwise stages of clinical drug development, from first-in-human safety testing (phase I) to post-marketing surveillance (phase IV).
items.body_md:
- Phase 0: optional microdosing/pharmacodynamic studies in very few patients.
- Phase I: first-in-human; safety, dose-limiting toxicities, maximum tolerated dose and recommended phase II dose (dose escalation, e.g. 3+3 design or model-based designs such as BOIN); in oncology usually in patients, with expansion cohorts.
- Phase II: efficacy signal (often objective response rate or PFS), single-arm or randomised; basket and umbrella designs.
- Phase III: randomised comparison against standard of care, primary endpoint usually OS or PFS; basis for approval.
- Phase IV: post-approval studies on long-term safety and real-world use.

Accelerated (FDA) or conditional (EMA) approvals may rest on phase II data with confirmatory trials required. Key concepts: randomisation, blinding, intention-to-treat analysis, non-inferiority vs superiority, stratification. Trial registries: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT numbers), EU Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS).

attrs.mnemonic: I = Is it safe? II = Does it work? III = Is it better than standard? IV = What happens in the real world?

items.gloss_md: The time from randomisation (or diagnosis/start of treatment) to death from any cause; the gold-standard endpoint in oncology.
items.body_md:
- Unambiguous and clinically meaningful; not affected by assessment bias.
- Drawbacks: needs large trials and long follow-up; diluted by subsequent therapies and crossover after progression.
- Reported as median OS (from Kaplan–Meier curves), landmark survival rates (e.g. 5-year OS) and hazard ratios from Cox models; patients alive at last contact are censored.

Reference values in PDAC: metastatic disease about 11 months with FOLFIRINOX (ACCORD 11, 11.1 vs 6.8 months for gemcitabine) and 8.5 months with gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel (MPACT); after resection with adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX, median OS 54.4 months (PRODIGE 24). Epidemiological "relative survival" in registries is a related but different measure (survival compared with the general population).

attrs.mnemonic: OS counts every death — it does not care why (Overall = 'Over and out').

items.gloss_md: The time from randomisation (or treatment start) to disease progression or death from any cause, whichever comes first.
items.body_md:
- Progression is usually defined by RECIST 1.1 on scheduled imaging (or clinical progression).
- Advantages over OS: earlier read-out, not confounded by subsequent lines of therapy, smaller trials.
- Limitations: depends on imaging schedule and assessor (blinded independent central review reduces bias), surrogate value for OS varies by tumour type, and a PFS gain does not always mean patients live longer or better (e.g. POLO: PFS 7.4 vs 3.8 months for olaparib, no OS difference).
- Related: time to progression (TTP, deaths without progression censored), time to treatment failure, PFS2 (progression on the next line).

In palliative settings PFS is the most common primary endpoint of phase III trials apart from OS.

attrs.mnemonic: PFS stops the clock at the first bad scan or death; OS waits for death only.

items.label_md: Disease-free survival (DFS) and related endpoints (RFS, EFS)
items.gloss_md: In patients rendered free of disease (e.g. after R0 resection), the time to recurrence, a new primary cancer or death; the typical endpoint of adjuvant trials.
items.body_md:
- DFS: recurrence, second primary cancer or death from any cause.
- RFS (recurrence-free survival): recurrence or death; definitions of what counts vary between trials, so read the protocol.
- EFS (event-free survival): used in neoadjuvant/perioperative trials; events include progression that precludes surgery, recurrence after surgery and death.
- pCR (pathological complete response): no residual invasive tumour in the specimen (ypT0 ypN0), a surrogate in breast and rectal cancer.

Examples: CONKO-001 (adjuvant gemcitabine) used DFS as primary endpoint; PRODIGE 24 (adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine) reported median DFS 21.6 vs 12.8 months. In German: krankheitsfreies Überleben.

attrs.mnemonic: DFS for the disease-free (after surgery), PFS for those still with disease (palliative).

items.label_md: Objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate
items.gloss_md: ORR is the proportion of patients with a complete or partial response by RECIST; disease control rate also counts stable disease.
items.body_md:
- ORR = (CR + PR) / evaluable patients. Usually requires confirmation of response on a later scan in single-arm trials.
- Disease control rate (DCR) = CR + PR + SD (often at a fixed time point).
- Duration of response (DoR): time from first response to progression; for accelerated approvals, durable responses matter more than ORR alone.
- Clinical benefit rate: similar to DCR with SD lasting ≥ a specified time (e.g. 24 weeks).

ORR is the typical primary endpoint of phase II and basket trials (e.g. sotorasib in *KRAS* G12C PDAC: ORR 21% in CodeBreaK 100). In PDAC, ORR to FOLFIRINOX is about 30% (ACCORD 11), to gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel about 23% (MPACT).

attrs.mnemonic: ORR = CR + PR (real shrinkage); DCR = ORR + SD (at least not growing).

items.gloss_md: The ratio of the instantaneous event rates (hazards) between two groups, usually estimated by a Cox proportional-hazards model; HR < 1 favours the experimental arm when events are bad outcomes.
items.body_md:
- Interpretation: HR 0.70 means a 30% lower instantaneous risk of the event (e.g. death) at any time point in the experimental arm, assuming proportional hazards.
- Reported with a 95% confidence interval and p value (log-rank test); a CI excluding 1 indicates a statistically significant difference.
- The HR is not a ratio of medians, although under exponential survival median ratio ≈ 1/HR.
- The proportional-hazards assumption fails when curves cross or separate late (typical for immunotherapy, which shows a delayed effect and a plateau); then restricted mean survival time (RMST) or milestone survival is more informative.

Examples: MPACT HR for death 0.72 (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel vs gemcitabine); POLO PFS HR 0.53 (olaparib vs placebo); NAPOLI-3 HR for death 0.83 (NALIRIFOX vs gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel).

attrs.mnemonic: HR below 1 = 'hazard reduced'; 1 − HR ≈ the relative risk reduction (0.72 → 28% lower hazard).
attrs.anecdote: David Cox published the proportional-hazards model in 1972 ('Regression models and life-tables'); it is one of the most cited statistics papers ever.

items.gloss_md: Evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of cancers, issued nationally (e.g. German S3 guidelines) and by international societies.
items.body_md:
- Germany: S3 guidelines of the Leitlinienprogramm Onkologie (AWMF, Deutsche Krebsgesellschaft, Deutsche Krebshilfe), e.g. the S3 guideline "Exokrines Pankreaskarzinom"; S3 is the highest level (systematic evidence review plus formal consensus). Onkopedia (DGHO) gives practical haematology/oncology guidance.
- USA: NCCN Guidelines (updated several times a year, define pancreatic resectability categories widely used worldwide), ASCO guidelines.
- Europe: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines with the ESMO Magnitude of Clinical Benefit Scale (ESMO-MCBS) and ESCAT.
- Evidence and recommendation grading: levels of evidence (Oxford, GRADE), recommendation strength ("soll", "sollte", "kann" in German guidelines).

Certified cancer centres must document guideline adherence via quality indicators derived from the S3 guidelines.

attrs.mnemonic: German 'soll – sollte – kann' = strong – moderate – open recommendation (shall – should – may).

items.label_md: Certified cancer centres in Germany (DKG, CCC)
items.gloss_md: German quality system in which the German Cancer Society (DKG) certifies organ cancer centres and oncology centres, and the German Cancer Aid funds Comprehensive Cancer Centres.
items.body_md:
- Organkrebszentren: organ-specific centres such as Pankreaskarzinomzentrum, Darmkrebszentrum, Leberkrebszentrum, as part of a Viszeralonkologisches Zentrum.
- Onkologisches Zentrum: covers several tumour entities in one institution.
- Comprehensive Cancer Centre (CCC): university-based centres combining care, research and teaching, funded by Deutsche Krebshilfe; the Nationales Centrum für Tumorerkrankungen (NCT) expanded to several sites.
- Requirements: minimum case numbers, presentation of all cases in a tumour board, quality indicators from S3 guidelines, annual audits, trial participation and documentation in the tumour documentation system.

Studies using German health insurance data (e.g. the WiZen study) found better survival for patients treated in certified centres. Note the abbreviation clash: "CCC" in German clinics can mean Comprehensive Cancer Center or cholangiocellular carcinoma.

items.gloss_md: A therapy-oriented grading of postoperative complications from grade I (minor deviation) to grade V (death).
items.body_md:
Dindo, Demartines and Clavien, Annals of Surgery 2004:
- Grade I: any deviation from the normal postoperative course without pharmacological, surgical, endoscopic or radiological intervention (allowed: antiemetics, antipyretics, analgesics, diuretics, electrolytes, physiotherapy, bedside opening of a wound infection).
- Grade II: requiring other drugs, blood transfusion or total parenteral nutrition.
- Grade III: requiring surgical, endoscopic or radiological intervention; IIIa without, IIIb under general anaesthesia.
- Grade IV: life-threatening, requiring ICU management; IVa single-organ, IVb multi-organ dysfunction.
- Grade V: death.
- Suffix "d" for disability at discharge.

"Major complications" usually means grade ≥IIIa or ≥IIIb. The Comprehensive Complication Index (CCI, 2013) sums all complications of a patient into a 0–100 score. Used across surgery including pancreatic surgery and liver transplantation.

attrs.mnemonic: Grade by the treatment needed: I nothing, II drugs, III intervention (a = awake, b = asleep), IV ICU, V death.

items.gloss_md: The most common pancreatic cancer (over 90% of cases), a malignant epithelial tumour with ductal differentiation that is usually diagnosed late and has one of the worst prognoses of all cancers.
items.body_md:
- Epidemiology: about 20,000 new cases per year in Germany, nearly as many deaths; median age at diagnosis around 70; incidence rising.
- Origin: precursor lesions (PanIN, IPMN, MCN) progress via *KRAS* activation and loss of *CDKN2A*, *TP53* and *SMAD4*.
- Pathology: infiltrating atypical glands in a dense desmoplastic stroma, frequent perineural and vascular invasion; about two thirds arise in the pancreatic head.
- Presentation: painless jaundice (head), weight loss, epigastric/back pain, new-onset diabetes.
- Staging: pancreatic-protocol CT, TNM 8th edition, NCCN resectability categories (resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced, metastatic).
- Treatment: resection (Whipple, distal or total pancreatectomy) plus adjuvant chemotherapy is the only chance of cure; only about 15–20% are resectable at diagnosis. Advanced disease: FOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel.
- Prognosis: 5-year survival about 10% overall.

German: duktales Adenokarzinom des Pankreas, colloquially Bauchspeicheldrüsenkrebs or Pankreaskarzinom.

attrs.anecdote: Ralph Steinman, who discovered dendritic cells, treated his own pancreatic cancer with experimental dendritic-cell vaccines; he died three days before being awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize, which the committee let stand although the prize is not normally given posthumously.

items.gloss_md: Pancreatic cancer is relatively uncommon in incidence but among the leading causes of cancer death because almost all patients die of the disease.
items.body_md:
- Germany: roughly 20,000 new cases per year (about 3–4% of all cancers) and almost as many deaths; one of the four leading causes of cancer death. Worldwide about half a million cases per year.
- USA: third leading cause of cancer death; projections (Rahib et al., Cancer Research 2014) suggested it would become the second around 2030.
- Incidence ≈ mortality: the mortality-to-incidence ratio is close to 1.
- Age: rare before 50, median age at diagnosis around 70–72 years; slightly more common in men.
- Trends: incidence is rising, partly because of ageing, obesity and diabetes; survival improves only slowly.
- Stage at diagnosis: about half metastatic, about a third locally advanced or borderline, only 15–20% resectable.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Incidence ≈ mortality': for PDAC the number diagnosed each year is almost the number who die each year.

items.gloss_md: Factors that increase the risk of PDAC: mainly smoking, obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic pancreatitis, family history and germline predisposition.
items.body_md:
- Smoking: the most important modifiable risk factor (about twofold risk; explains up to a quarter of cases).
- Obesity, physical inactivity, metabolic syndrome; type 2 diabetes (long-standing diabetes moderately raises risk; new-onset diabetes can be an early sign of the cancer).
- Chronic pancreatitis (several-fold risk), heavy alcohol intake (mainly via pancreatitis).
- Family history: familial pancreatic cancer (≥2 first-degree relatives) and germline variants (*BRCA2*, *BRCA1*, *PALB2*, *ATM*, *CDKN2A*, *STK11*, mismatch-repair genes); hereditary pancreatitis (*PRSS1*) carries a very high lifetime risk.
- Precursor cysts: IPMN and MCN.
- Others: age, non-O blood group (*ABO* locus in GWAS), *Helicobacter pylori*, high red and processed meat intake (weaker evidence).

Screening of the general population is not recommended because incidence is low; surveillance is offered to high-risk individuals.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Smoke, Sugar, Size, Sore pancreas, Siblings': smoking, diabetes, obesity, chronic pancreatitis, family history.

items.gloss_md: PDAC presents late with painless obstructive jaundice (head tumours), weight loss, epigastric or back pain and sometimes new-onset diabetes.
items.body_md:
- Pancreatic head tumours (about two thirds): painless jaundice from compression of the distal common bile duct, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus; Courvoisier sign (palpable, non-tender gallbladder).
- Body/tail tumours: no jaundice, so they present later with pain and weight loss; more often metastatic.
- Epigastric pain radiating to the back suggests coeliac plexus or retroperitoneal invasion and often unresectability.
- Weight loss and cachexia, anorexia, early satiety (gastric outlet obstruction), steatorrhoea (exocrine insufficiency).
- New-onset diabetes in people over 50, acute pancreatitis without another cause.
- Thromboembolism (Trousseau syndrome), depression.

On imaging: hypoattenuating mass, "double duct sign" (dilated common bile duct and pancreatic duct). Symptoms are non-specific, contributing to delayed diagnosis.

attrs.mnemonic: Courvoisier's law: 'a palpable gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be stones' — stones scar the gallbladder so it cannot distend; a tumour blocks slowly and lets it swell.
attrs.anecdote: Ludwig Georg Courvoisier, a Swiss surgeon, formulated the observation in 1890 from his series of patients with common bile duct obstruction.

items.gloss_md: A sialylated Lewis-a blood-group antigen measured in serum as the standard tumour marker for pancreatic cancer, used for monitoring and prognosis but not for screening.
items.body_md:
- Upper limit of normal usually 37 U/mL.
- Diagnostic performance in symptomatic patients: sensitivity and specificity roughly 80%; too low for screening the general population.
- False positives: biliary obstruction and cholangitis (measure again after biliary drainage), pancreatitis, liver cirrhosis, other GI and gynaecological cancers.
- False negatives: Lewis-negative individuals (about 5–10% of people) cannot synthesise CA19-9.
- Prognostic uses: very high preoperative levels (e.g. >500 U/mL) suggest occult metastatic disease and are a "biological" borderline-resectable criterion; normalisation after resection or a decline under chemotherapy predicts better survival; rising levels often precede radiological recurrence.

CA19-9 was identified by Koprowski and colleagues in 1979 with a monoclonal antibody raised against a colorectal cancer cell line. Also elevated in cholangiocarcinoma and used there similarly.

attrs.mnemonic: '37 is the limit': like a fever at 37 °C, CA19-9 above 37 U/mL is abnormal; but jaundice also 'heats it up'.
attrs.anecdote: CA19-9 was discovered with one of the first monoclonal antibodies used in cancer research, made by Hilary Koprowski's group at the Wistar Institute only four years after the invention of hybridomas.

items.label_md: Imaging of pancreatic cancer (pancreatic-protocol CT, MRI, PET)
items.gloss_md: Multiphase pancreatic-protocol contrast CT is the standard for diagnosis and staging of PDAC, complemented by MRI for liver metastases and endoscopic ultrasound.
items.body_md:
- Pancreatic-protocol CT: thin slices (≤3 mm), pancreatic parenchymal (late arterial) phase to maximise tumour–pancreas contrast and portal-venous phase for veins and liver; multiplanar reconstructions to assess contact with the SMA, coeliac axis, CHA, SMV and portal vein in degrees (≤180° vs >180°). Chest CT completes staging.
- Findings: hypoattenuating ill-defined mass, double-duct sign, upstream duct dilatation and parenchymal atrophy; about 10% of tumours are isoattenuating and visible only indirectly.
- MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging and hepatobiliary contrast detects small liver metastases missed by CT.
- FDG-PET/CT is not routine but may detect occult metastases, especially in high-risk cases.
- Imaging should precede biliary stenting (stent artefacts and post-ERCP pancreatitis impair staging).
- Structured radiology reports (e.g. the SAR/APA template) standardise vascular assessment.

After neoadjuvant therapy, CT often overestimates residual tumour because fibrosis looks like tumour; resectability decisions then rely also on CA19-9 and clinical response.

attrs.mnemonic: Double-duct sign = two dilated tubes (bile duct + pancreatic duct) pointing at one blockage in the head.

items.gloss_md: Classification of non-metastatic PDAC by tumour contact with major vessels into resectable, borderline resectable and locally advanced (unresectable), with metastatic disease as a fourth category.
items.body_md:
Based on pancreatic-protocol CT (NCCN, aligned with the 2017 international consensus):
- Resectable: no arterial contact (coeliac axis, SMA, common hepatic artery); no contact with SMV/portal vein or ≤180° contact without vein contour irregularity.
- Borderline resectable (BR): venous involvement that can be reconstructed (>180° SMV/PV contact, or ≤180° with contour irregularity or thrombosis), or limited arterial contact (CHA without extension to coeliac axis or hepatic bifurcation; SMA ≤180°; for body/tail tumours coeliac axis ≤180°).
- Locally advanced (LAPC): >180° contact with SMA or coeliac axis, aortic involvement with coeliac axis contact, or unreconstructible SMV/PV.
- Metastatic: distant metastases including non-regional lymph nodes and peritoneal disease.

Treatment logic: resectable → upfront surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy (or neoadjuvant in high-risk cases); BR → neoadjuvant therapy, then surgery; LAPC → induction chemotherapy, conversion surgery in selected responders; metastatic → palliative systemic therapy. The international (IAP 2018) definition adds biological (CA19-9 >500 U/mL, suspected metastases) and conditional (ECOG ≥2) factors.

attrs.mnemonic: Arteries decide 'no', veins decide 'maybe': arterial encasement >180° = locally advanced; veins can be reconstructed = borderline. 180° = half the vessel's circumference.

items.label_md: TNM staging of pancreatic cancer (8th edition)
items.gloss_md: The UICC/AJCC 8th edition stages exocrine pancreatic cancer by tumour size, arterial involvement and number of positive lymph nodes.
items.body_md:
- T1: ≤2 cm (T1a ≤0.5 cm, T1b >0.5–1 cm, T1c >1–2 cm).
- T2: >2 and ≤4 cm.
- T3: >4 cm.
- T4: involvement of the coeliac axis, superior mesenteric artery and/or common hepatic artery, regardless of size.
- N0: no regional nodes; N1: 1–3 positive regional nodes; N2: ≥4 positive nodes.
- M1: distant metastasis.

Stage groups: IA T1N0; IB T2N0; IIA T3N0; IIB T1–3 N1; III T4 any N or any T N2; IV M1.

Changes from the 7th edition: T is now size-based (extension beyond the pancreas no longer defines T3), and N is split into N1/N2 by node count. At least 12 examined nodes are recommended. Tis = high-grade PanIN (or high-grade dysplasia in IPMN/MCN). Pancreatic NETs have their own TNM.

attrs.mnemonic: T by 2-4: ≤2, 2–4, >4 cm, T4 = arteries (CA, SMA, CHA); N by 1-3-4: N1 = 1–3 nodes, N2 = ≥4.

items.gloss_md: PDAC has the lowest 5-year survival of the common cancers (about 10% overall), with clear differences by stage and treatment.
items.body_md:
- Overall 5-year relative survival: about 10% in Germany and roughly 13% in recent US statistics.
- Metastatic disease: median OS about 8–12 months with modern chemotherapy (3–4 months untreated); 5-year survival in the low single digits.
- Locally advanced: median OS about 1–2 years with induction chemotherapy; longer if conversion resection is possible.
- Resected: median OS about 2–4.5 years depending on adjuvant regimen and selection (54 months with mFOLFIRINOX in fit patients in PRODIGE 24); still most patients relapse, mainly in the liver and locally.

Prognostic factors: stage, R status, nodal status (N2), grade, CA19-9 level and kinetics, performance status, molecular subtype (basal-like worse), response to neoadjuvant therapy, treatment at high-volume centres. Long-term survivors exist and are enriched for strong anti-tumour T-cell responses.

attrs.mnemonic: 'One in ten at five years' overall; 'four and a half years' median after resection and mFOLFIRINOX; 'under a year' when metastatic.

items.gloss_md: PDAC is driven by four frequently altered genes: *KRAS* activation in over 90% and inactivation of *CDKN2A*, *TP53* and *SMAD4*, plus a long tail of rarer alterations.
items.body_md:
- *KRAS*: activating mutations in about 90–95%, almost always at codon 12 (G12D most common, then G12V and G12R; G12C only about 1–2%) or less often Q61/G13.
- *CDKN2A*: inactivated in about 90% (mutation, homozygous deletion often with *MTAP*, or promoter methylation), loss of p16INK4a.
- *TP53*: mutated in about 70%, mostly missense.
- *SMAD4*: inactivated in about 50%; loss associated with widespread metastatic disease (Iacobuzio-Donahue et al. 2009).
- Lower-frequency: chromatin remodelling (*ARID1A*, *KDM6A*), *RNF43*, *TGFBR2*, DNA repair genes (*BRCA1/2*, *PALB2*, *ATM*), *GNAS* (IPMN-derived), *MYC* amplification.
- *KRAS*-wild-type tumours (8–10%): enriched for targetable fusions (*NRG1*, *NTRK*, *ALK*, *RET*), *BRAF* alterations and MSI.
- Germline pathogenic variants: about 5–10% of unselected patients.

Low tumour mutational burden (~1–2 mut/Mb) and low purity are typical. Reference projects: Jones et al. (Science 2008), TCGA PAAD (2017), ICGC/APGI (Bailey 2016), COMPASS.

attrs.mnemonic: The 'Big Four' with frequencies ~90-90-70-50: KRAS 90+, CDKN2A 90, TP53 70, SMAD4 50 — 'one accelerator, three broken brakes'.
attrs.anecdote: Jones et al. (Science 2008) sequenced 24 PDACs and found an average of 63 genetic alterations in 12 core pathways — one of the first exome-scale cancer studies, using Sanger sequencing.

items.label_md: Metastatic pancreatic cancer and first-line treatment
items.gloss_md: Stage IV PDAC (about half of patients at diagnosis) is treated with palliative combination chemotherapy chosen mainly by performance status and biomarkers.
items.body_md:
Typical metastatic sites: liver, peritoneum, lungs, distant nodes. Biopsy (often of a liver lesion) confirms the diagnosis and provides tissue for molecular profiling; germline testing and somatic NGS are recommended.

First-line options:
- ECOG 0–1, fit, normal bilirubin: FOLFIRINOX (ACCORD 11) or NALIRIFOX (NAPOLI-3).
- ECOG 0–2: gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel (MPACT).
- ECOG 2 or frail: gemcitabine monotherapy (± capecitabine), dose-reduced combinations.
- ECOG 3–4: best supportive care.
- g*BRCA*/*PALB2*: platinum-based induction followed by olaparib maintenance (g*BRCA*).
- MSI-H/dMMR: checkpoint inhibitor.

Second line depends on the first (gemcitabine-based ↔ fluoropyrimidine-based). Supportive care (pain, nutrition, PERT, biliary stenting, thromboprophylaxis, early palliative care) is integral. Patients with lung-only metastases have a notably better prognosis.

attrs.mnemonic: Fit → FOLFIRINOX/NALIRIFOX, less fit → Gem/nab-P, frail → Gem, bedridden → BSC: 'the fitter the patient, the more drugs'.

items.gloss_md: The pancreas is a retroperitoneal gland with head, uncinate process, neck, body and tail, an exocrine part (acini and ducts) and an endocrine part (islets of Langerhans).
items.body_md:
- Head: within the C-loop of the duodenum; the distal common bile duct runs through it. Uncinate process: hooks behind the superior mesenteric vein. Neck: lies in front of the SMV–portal vein confluence. Body: crosses the aorta and SMA origin. Tail: reaches the splenic hilum.
- Ducts: the main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) joins the common bile duct at the ampulla of Vater and opens at the major duodenal papilla; the accessory duct (duct of Santorini) drains via the minor papilla.
- Exocrine (~98% of mass): acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, trypsinogen, elastase); ductal cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid (CFTR).
- Endocrine (~1–2%): islets with β cells (insulin), α cells (glucagon), δ cells (somatostatin), PP cells (pancreatic polypeptide), ε cells (ghrelin).
- Blood supply: head from the gastroduodenal artery (superior pancreaticoduodenal arcades) and SMA (inferior arcades); body/tail from the splenic artery.

Tumour location determines the operation: head → pancreatoduodenectomy, body/tail → distal pancreatectomy.

attrs.mnemonic: Head–neck–body–tail like a lying animal whose head rests in the duodenal 'C', with its tail pointing to the spleen.
attrs.anecdote: Paul Langerhans described the islets in his 1869 doctoral thesis in Berlin as a medical student, without knowing their function.

items.gloss_md: The arteries (coeliac axis, common hepatic artery, SMA) and veins (SMV, portal vein) around the pancreas whose involvement determines resectability.
items.body_md:
- Coeliac axis (truncus coeliacus): from the aorta at about T12; branches into the common hepatic artery (CHA), splenic artery and left gastric artery.
- CHA → gastroduodenal artery (GDA, runs in front of the pancreatic head; its stump is ligated in a Whipple and is a source of late haemorrhage) and proper hepatic artery.
- Superior mesenteric artery (SMA): from the aorta about 1 cm below the coeliac axis, behind the pancreatic neck; surrounded by a nerve plexus, a route of perineural spread.
- Superior mesenteric vein (SMV) joins the splenic vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein (PV); first jejunal vein branches matter for venous reconstruction.
- Variants: a replaced right hepatic artery from the SMA (roughly one in ten patients) runs behind the pancreatic head and must be recognised preoperatively.

Radiology reports describe tumour contact in degrees of circumference (≤180° "abutment" vs >180° "encasement"), contour deformity and thrombosis.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Abutment ≤180°, encasement >180°': abut = touch, encase = wrap around.

items.gloss_md: Non-metastatic PDAC with vessel involvement that makes upfront R0 resection unlikely but resection possible after neoadjuvant therapy, usually with venous reconstruction.
items.body_md:
NCCN anatomical criteria:
- Pancreatic head/uncinate: tumour contact with the CHA without extension to the coeliac axis or hepatic artery bifurcation; SMA contact ≤180°; contact with variant arterial anatomy.
- Body/tail: coeliac axis contact ≤180° (or >180° without aortic involvement and with an intact GDA, which some classify as locally advanced).
- Veins: SMV/PV contact >180°, or ≤180° with contour irregularity or thrombosis, provided reconstruction is possible; IVC contact.

International (IAP, Isaji 2018) "ABC" concept: Anatomical (A), Biological (B: CA19-9 >500 U/mL or regional lymph-node metastases on biopsy/PET) and Conditional (C: ECOG ≥2) borderline resectability.

Standard: neoadjuvant chemotherapy (mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel, ± chemoradiation) for 2–6 months, then restaging and surgical exploration in the absence of progression; R0 rates and survival improve compared with upfront surgery (supported by randomised data, e.g. the Korean and PREOPANC trials).

attrs.mnemonic: ABC of borderline: Anatomy, Biology (CA19-9 >500), Condition (ECOG ≥2).

items.gloss_md: Non-metastatic PDAC that is unresectable at diagnosis because of arterial encasement (>180° SMA or coeliac axis) or unreconstructible venous involvement.
items.body_md:
About 30% of patients present with LAPC.

- Treatment: induction chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel) for at least 4–6 months, then multidisciplinary restaging. Options afterwards: continued chemotherapy, maintenance, chemoradiation or SBRT for local control, or surgical exploration.
- Conversion resection: possible in selected responders at experienced centres, sometimes with arterial resection or the TRIANGLE operation; survival after successful resection approaches that of initially resectable disease.
- Response assessment is difficult: CT rarely shows shrinkage because fibrosis persists; decreasing CA19-9, improved performance status and metabolic response on PET favour exploration.
