- LAP07 (Hammel et al., JAMA 2016): chemoradiation after 4 months of gemcitabine-based induction did not improve OS compared with continued chemotherapy, but reduced local progression.

Prognosis: median OS around 1.5–2 years with modern chemotherapy.

attrs.mnemonic: Locally advanced = 'locked arteries': SMA or coeliac axis wrapped more than half-way (>180°).

items.gloss_md: Endoscopic ultrasound from the stomach or duodenum that images the pancreas at high resolution and obtains cytology (FNA) or core tissue (FNB) from lesions.
items.body_md:
- Detects small tumours (<2 cm) missed by CT and assesses vessel involvement and lymph nodes.
- FNA (fine-needle aspiration) yields cytology; FNB needles (Franseen, fork-tip designs) yield tissue cores for histology, IHC and molecular profiling (NGS, organoids). Diagnostic sensitivity for PDAC is about 85–90%, specificity close to 100%; a negative result does not exclude cancer.
- Indications: tissue diagnosis before neoadjuvant or palliative therapy (mandatory), unclear masses (autoimmune pancreatitis, NET, lymphoma, metastases), cyst evaluation (fluid CEA, cytology, mural nodules, contrast-enhanced EUS).
- Tissue confirmation is not required before upfront resection of a typical resectable mass.
- Therapeutic EUS: coeliac plexus neurolysis for pain, EUS-guided biliary drainage and gastroenterostomy.
- Complications: pancreatitis, bleeding, infection (cysts), rarely needle-tract seeding (lower for head lesions because the tract is resected in a Whipple).

attrs.mnemonic: FNA = Aspirate cells (cytology), FNB = Biopsy cores (histology).

items.label_md: ERCP and biliary drainage in pancreatic cancer
items.gloss_md: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stent placement to relieve malignant biliary obstruction caused by a pancreatic head tumour.
items.body_md:
- Preoperative biliary drainage: routine drainage before early surgery increases complications (van der Gaag et al., NEJM 2010), so it is reserved for cholangitis, very high bilirubin, pruritus, delayed surgery or planned neoadjuvant therapy.
- Stent choice: self-expanding metal stents (SEMS, often fully covered) stay open longer than plastic stents and are preferred for neoadjuvant and palliative patients.
- Palliative: SEMS for jaundice; duodenal stents or (EUS-guided) gastroenterostomy for gastric outlet obstruction.
- Alternatives: percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) or EUS-guided drainage when ERCP fails.
- Complications: post-ERCP pancreatitis, cholangitis, stent occlusion, perforation.

Brush cytology from strictures has low sensitivity; CT should be done before stenting. Bilirubin must normalise before chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX, irinotecan) and before CA19-9 can be interpreted.

items.gloss_md: Diagnostic laparoscopy before planned resection to detect occult peritoneal or liver surface metastases not seen on imaging.
items.body_md:
In PDAC, radiologically occult metastases are found in a relevant minority of patients thought to be resectable, more often with large tumours, body/tail location, very high CA19-9 (e.g. >500 U/mL), ascites or after neoadjuvant therapy. Peritoneal washing cytology can be added (positive cytology counts as M1).

Benefit: spares a futile laparotomy and allows earlier start of chemotherapy. It is recommended selectively in guidelines (NCCN: consider in high-risk patients) rather than for all. It is also used in gastric cancer before perioperative chemotherapy.

items.gloss_md: The standard resection for tumours of the pancreatic head and periampullary region, removing the pancreatic head, duodenum, distal bile duct, gallbladder and (classically) the distal stomach.
items.body_md:
- Resection (classic Kausch–Whipple): pancreatic head with uncinate process, duodenum, first jejunal loop, distal common bile duct, gallbladder, antrum of the stomach, and regional lymph nodes (standard lymphadenectomy along hepatoduodenal ligament, CHA, SMA right side).
- Reconstruction (three anastomoses): pancreaticojejunostomy (or pancreaticogastrostomy), hepaticojejunostomy, gastrojejunostomy (duodenojejunostomy in the pylorus-preserving variant).
- Variants: pylorus-preserving pancreatoduodenectomy (PPPD; standard in many German centres), pylorus-resecting PD, with portal vein resection, laparoscopic or robotic.
- Outcomes: mortality <3–5% at high-volume centres but higher nationally (older German nationwide data around 10% in-hospital mortality for pancreatic resections); morbidity 40–60%.
- Key complications: postoperative pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, post-pancreatectomy haemorrhage, bile leak, abscess; long-term exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.

German colloquial: Whipple-OP, Kausch-Whipple-Operation, partielle Duodenopankreatektomie.

attrs.mnemonic: Three anastomoses after a Whipple, from top to bottom: pancreas, bile duct, stomach — 'P-B-S: Pancreas, Bile, Stomach'.
attrs.anecdote: Walther Kausch performed the first successful two-stage pancreatoduodenectomy in Berlin in 1909; Allen Oldfather Whipple in New York popularised the operation from 1935 — hence 'Kausch–Whipple' in Germany and just 'Whipple' in English.

items.gloss_md: A modification of the Whipple operation that keeps the entire stomach and pylorus with a short cuff of duodenum, reconstructed by duodenojejunostomy.
items.body_md:
Described by Traverso and Longmire in 1978 (Watson had reported it earlier, in 1944).

- Rationale: preserves gastric reservoir and pyloric function, avoiding dumping and possibly improving nutrition.
- Oncology: survival and R0 rates are equivalent to the classic Whipple for appropriately selected tumours (not when the tumour involves the pylorus or proximal duodenum).
- Delayed gastric emptying: initially thought more frequent; meta-analyses and the German PROPP trial (pylorus-resecting vs pylorus-preserving, Hackert et al. 2018) found no significant difference.

PPPD is the most common pancreatic head resection in many German centres; in reports the abbreviation "PPPD" usually means this operation (not a disease).

items.gloss_md: Resection of the pancreatic body and tail, usually with splenectomy for cancer, for tumours left of the SMV–portal vein axis.
items.body_md:
- Oncological resection for PDAC includes splenectomy (splenic vessels and hilar nodes); spleen-preserving techniques are used for benign or low-grade lesions.
- Radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy (RAMPS, Strasberg 2003) improves posterior margin clearance.
- Distal pancreatectomy with coeliac axis resection (DP-CAR, modified Appleby procedure) for body tumours involving the coeliac axis; liver perfusion is maintained via the SMA–pancreaticoduodenal arcades–GDA.
- Minimally invasive (laparoscopic, robotic) distal pancreatectomy is widely used; the DIPLOMA trial showed non-inferior radicality for laparoscopic vs open resection in cancer.
- Main complication: postoperative pancreatic fistula from the pancreatic stump (more frequent than after Whipple; stapler or suture closure); no digestive anastomosis is needed.
- After splenectomy: vaccinations against encapsulated bacteria (pneumococci, meningococci, Haemophilus).

Body/tail PDAC is often diagnosed later and is less frequently resectable.

attrs.mnemonic: Germans resect 'links' (left): Pankreaslinksresektion = distal pancreatectomy (tail lies to the patient's left).

items.gloss_md: Removal of the entire pancreas (with duodenum, distal bile duct, spleen and often part of the stomach), producing complete exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.
items.body_md:
Indications: tumours extending through the whole gland, main-duct IPMN involving the entire duct, repeatedly positive pancreatic neck margin on frozen section, multifocal neoplasms (e.g. hereditary), or as a bail-out when a safe pancreatic anastomosis is impossible (very soft gland, severe pancreatitis or fistula complications).

Consequences: insulin-dependent pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes that is often "brittle" because glucagon is also lost (hypoglycaemia risk); lifelong pancreatic enzyme replacement. Modern diabetes technology (continuous glucose monitoring, insulin pumps) has improved quality of life; total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation is used for benign chronic pancreatitis, not cancer. Perioperative mortality is now comparable to Whipple at experienced centres, as no pancreatic anastomosis can leak.

items.label_md: Vascular resection in pancreatic surgery (venous, arterial, TRIANGLE)
items.gloss_md: Resection and reconstruction of the SMV/portal vein or, rarely, of arteries during pancreatectomy to achieve tumour clearance.
items.body_md:
- Venous resection: tangential (wedge) or segmental resection of the SMV/portal vein with primary anastomosis or interposition graft (e.g. left renal vein, jugular vein, synthetic); standard at high-volume centres for borderline-resectable tumours, with survival similar to standard resection when R0 is achieved.
- Arterial resection (SMA, CHA, coeliac axis): high morbidity and mortality, considered only after good response to neoadjuvant therapy at specialised centres; DP-CAR for coeliac axis involvement in body tumours.
- TRIANGLE operation (Hackert et al., Heidelberg, 2017): after neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced PDAC, complete removal of all soft tissue in the triangle bounded by the coeliac axis/CHA, SMA and SMV–portal vein, including periarterial nerve plexus, without arterial resection, based on the idea that post-therapy tissue around the arteries is often fibrotic rather than tumour.
- "Artery-first" approaches dissect the SMA early to judge resectability before irreversible steps.

items.gloss_md: Leakage of pancreatic juice from the pancreatic anastomosis or stump after pancreatic surgery, defined by drain amylase >3× the serum upper normal limit from postoperative day 3 with clinical relevance.
items.body_md:
ISGPS/ISGPF definition (Bassi et al. 2005, updated 2016):
- Biochemical leak (BL, formerly grade A): drain amylase >3× upper limit of normal serum amylase on or after postoperative day 3 without clinical impact; no longer counted as a true fistula.
- Grade B: clinically relevant, requires a change in management: persistent drainage >3 weeks, percutaneous or endoscopic drainage, angiographic intervention for related bleeding, or signs of infection without organ failure.
- Grade C: reoperation, single or multiple organ failure, or death related to the fistula.

Incidence of clinically relevant POPF: roughly 10–20% after Whipple and higher after distal pancreatectomy. Risk factors (Fistula Risk Score, Callery 2013): soft gland texture, small duct diameter (≤3 mm), high-risk pathology (not PDAC or pancreatitis, e.g. ampullary, duodenal, cystic, NET), high intraoperative blood loss. PDAC with a hard, fibrotic gland and dilated duct has a lower fistula risk. Consequences: abscess, erosion bleeding (post-pancreatectomy haemorrhage), delayed adjuvant therapy.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Three times, day three': drain amylase >3× normal from POD 3. BL = biochemistry only; B = 'Behandlung' changes; C = 'Catastrophe' (reoperation, organ failure, death).

items.gloss_md: Impaired gastric emptying after pancreatic surgery, graded A–C by the ISGPS according to how long a nasogastric tube is needed and when solid food is tolerated.
items.body_md:
ISGPS definition (Wente et al., Surgery 2007):
- Grade A: nasogastric tube (NGT) required for 4–7 days or reinsertion after postoperative day (POD) 3, or inability to tolerate solid oral intake by POD 7.
- Grade B: NGT 8–14 days or reinsertion after POD 7, or no solid intake by POD 14.
- Grade C: NGT >14 days or reinsertion after POD 14, or no solid intake by POD 21.

One of the most frequent complications after pancreatoduodenectomy (reported in roughly 15–30%). It is often secondary to intra-abdominal complications such as fistula or abscess. Management: gastric decompression, prokinetics (erythromycin, metoclopramide), nutritional support (jejunal tube or parenteral). Pylorus preservation vs resection does not clearly change DGE rates (PROPP trial).

attrs.mnemonic: DGE grades follow the week: A by day 7, B by day 14, C by day 21 (solid food).

items.gloss_md: Bleeding after pancreatic resection, classified by the ISGPS by timing (early ≤24 h, late >24 h), location (intra- or extraluminal) and severity into grades A–C.
items.body_md:
- Early PPH (≤24 h): usually technical (inadequate haemostasis, coagulopathy), treated by relaparotomy.
- Late PPH (>24 h, often days to weeks): typically erosion of a vessel (gastroduodenal artery stump, hepatic artery, SMA branches) by pancreatic juice from a fistula or abscess, with pseudoaneurysm formation; associated with high mortality.
- Sentinel bleed: a small, self-limiting bleed (via drain or GI tract) that often precedes massive haemorrhage; requires urgent CT angiography.
- Treatment of late bleeding: interventional angiography (coil embolisation, covered stent) as first choice, or surgery.

Grading (Wente et al. 2007): A mild early bleeding without clinical impact; B requires transfusion or intervention (or mild late bleeding); C severe late bleeding, life-threatening, needs angiographic intervention or relaparotomy.

items.label_md: Resection margins in pancreatic cancer (1 mm rule)
items.gloss_md: In PDAC, a resection is often classified as R1 if tumour cells lie within 1 mm of a resection margin, not only at the margin itself.
items.body_md:
- Margins of a Whipple specimen: pancreatic neck (transection), bile duct, gastric/duodenal, and circumferential resection margins (CRM): SMA margin (most often involved), SMV/PV groove, posterior and anterior surfaces.
- Standardised pathology (Leeds Pathology Protocol, axial slicing, multicolour inking) increased reported R1 rates from about 20% to over 70% in some series, because PDAC grows diffusely and discontinuously.
- Definitions differ: "R1 direct" (0 mm, tumour at margin; UICC/CAP) vs "R1 <1 mm" (UK RCPath, many European centres). German reports often state "R0 (CRM−)" for ≥1 mm clearance and "R0 (CRM+)" or "R0 narrow" for <1 mm.
- Prognosis: ≥1 mm clearance is associated with better survival in many studies.

When comparing trials, check which definition was used; adjuvant trials (e.g. PRODIGE 24, ESPAC-4) included both R0 and R1 patients.

attrs.mnemonic: 'One millimetre makes the difference': <1 mm = R1 in the 1-mm world, R0 in the UICC/CAP world.

items.gloss_md: Microscopic (<5 mm) non-invasive neoplastic lesions of small pancreatic ducts that are the main precursor of PDAC.
items.body_md:
- Size and visibility: by definition usually <5 mm, flat or micropapillary, mucinous columnar epithelium; not visible on imaging (unlike IPMN).
- Grading (Baltimore consensus 2015, WHO 2019): two-tier low-grade PanIN (formerly PanIN-1A, 1B and 2) and high-grade PanIN (formerly PanIN-3, carcinoma in situ, staged Tis).
- Genetics: *KRAS* mutations already in most low-grade PanINs (and telomere shortening); *CDKN2A* loss in intermediate lesions; *TP53* and *SMAD4* loss mainly in high-grade PanIN and invasive cancer.
- Low-grade PanIN is very common in older adults and mostly does not progress; high-grade PanIN is rare and usually found next to invasive cancer.

PanIN progression is the basis of the PDAC progression model (Hruban et al. 2000) and is recapitulated in the KC mouse model. Arises partly from acinar cells via acinar-to-ductal metaplasia.

attrs.mnemonic: PanIN is 'in' the duct and invisible ('tiny, <5 mm, no imaging'); IPMN is the big visible cyst.

items.gloss_md: A mucin-producing, papillary neoplasm growing within the main pancreatic duct and/or its branches, visible as a cystic lesion communicating with the duct, and a precursor of pancreatic cancer.
items.body_md:
- Types: main-duct (MD-IPMN; segmental or diffuse dilatation of the main duct ≥5 mm without other cause), branch-duct (BD-IPMN; cyst >5 mm communicating with the main duct), and mixed type.
- Malignancy risk: high for main-duct involvement (in resected series on average about 60% harboured high-grade dysplasia or invasion), much lower for branch-duct IPMN (often managed by surveillance).
- Epithelial subtypes: gastric (mostly BD, low risk), intestinal (often MD, associated with colloid carcinoma), pancreatobiliary (associated with tubular, PDAC-like carcinoma); oncocytic neoplasms are now a separate entity (IOPN).
- Genetics: *KRAS* and *GNAS* (codon 201) mutations; *RNF43* loss. *GNAS* in cyst fluid is fairly specific for IPMN.
- Endoscopy: mucin extruding from a patulous "fish-mouth" papilla in MD-IPMN.
- Management: risk-stratified by the Fukuoka/Kyoto (international) or European guidelines; resection for high-risk stigmata, surveillance for low-risk BD-IPMN. Invasive cancer can arise from the IPMN or concomitantly elsewhere in the gland, so lifelong follow-up is needed even after resection.

IPMNs are frequent incidental findings on CT/MRI, especially in older people.

attrs.mnemonic: Main duct = main danger; branch duct = mostly benign (watch it).
attrs.anecdote: IPMNs were described as a distinct entity by Ohhashi and colleagues in Japan in 1982 as 'mucin-producing cancer' with a dilated papilla, which is why Japanese groups have shaped the international (Sendai, Fukuoka, Kyoto) guidelines.

items.label_md: Fukuoka and Kyoto guidelines for IPMN (high-risk stigmata, worrisome features)
items.gloss_md: International consensus guidelines that stratify IPMN by high-risk stigmata (usually resect) and worrisome features (further evaluation by EUS) to decide between resection and surveillance.
items.body_md:
Lineage: Sendai (2006) → Fukuoka (2012, revised 2017) → Kyoto (2024).

Fukuoka 2017:
- High-risk stigmata: obstructive jaundice with a cystic lesion of the pancreatic head; enhancing mural nodule ≥5 mm; main pancreatic duct ≥10 mm.
- Worrisome features: pancreatitis; cyst ≥3 cm; enhancing mural nodule <5 mm; thickened or enhancing cyst wall; main duct 5–9 mm; abrupt change in duct calibre with distal atrophy; lymphadenopathy; elevated serum CA19-9; cyst growth ≥5 mm in 2 years.

Kyoto 2024 refinements include positive or suspicious cytology as a high-risk stigma, new-onset or worsening diabetes as a worrisome feature, and a cyst growth rate of ≥2.5 mm per year.

The European evidence-based guidelines (2018) use similar "absolute" and "relative" indications (e.g. relative: growth ≥5 mm/year, CA19-9 >37 U/mL, MPD 5–9.9 mm, cyst ≥40 mm, new-onset diabetes, acute pancreatitis, enhancing nodule <5 mm).

attrs.mnemonic: High-risk stigmata '5–10–jaundice': nodule ≥5 mm, main duct ≥10 mm, jaundice. Worrisome = the 'half-way' values: nodule <5, duct 5–9, cyst ≥3 cm.

items.label_md: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas (MCN)
items.gloss_md: A mucin-producing cystic neoplasm with ovarian-type stroma, almost exclusively in women, typically in the pancreatic body or tail, and a precursor of invasive carcinoma.
items.body_md:
- Patients: >95% women, usually middle-aged (40s–50s).
- Location: body/tail; usually unilocular or septated "cyst within a cyst" with a thick wall, sometimes peripheral eggshell calcification.
- Defining feature: ovarian-type subepithelial stroma (oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive); no communication with the pancreatic duct (distinguishes it from IPMN).
- Dysplasia graded low vs high; invasive carcinoma in a minority, more likely with large size, mural nodules or thick walls.
- Management: resection (usually distal pancreatectomy, often minimally invasive and spleen-preserving) for MCN ≥4 cm, symptoms or risk features; small ones without risk features may be observed (European guidelines). Non-invasive MCNs are cured by resection and need no follow-up.

attrs.mnemonic: MCN = 'Mother's Cystic Neoplasm': women, ovarian stroma, tail of the pancreas, no duct connection.

items.gloss_md: Cystic lesions of the pancreas range from inflammatory pseudocysts to benign serous cystadenomas and mucinous precursors of cancer (IPMN, MCN).
items.body_md:
- Pseudocyst: after pancreatitis, no epithelial lining, high amylase in fluid.
- Serous cystadenoma (SCA): microcystic "honeycomb" with a central scar or calcification, typical in older women, almost always benign; associated with *VHL*; usually observed.
- IPMN: communicates with the duct; mucinous; *KRAS*/*GNAS*.
- MCN: women, body/tail, ovarian-type stroma, no duct communication.
- Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN): young women, solid-cystic, *CTNNB1* (β-catenin) mutations, low-grade malignant; resection is curative in most cases.
- Cystic degeneration of NETs or PDAC.

Work-up: MRI/MRCP (duct communication, nodules), EUS with fine-needle aspiration of cyst fluid: CEA >192 ng/mL suggests a mucinous cyst; low glucose (<50 mg/dL) is also suggestive of mucinous lesions; cytology; DNA testing (*KRAS*, *GNAS*, *VHL*, *TP53*). Incidental cysts are found in a considerable proportion of older adults on MRI.

attrs.mnemonic: Cyst fluid CEA high = mucinous (IPMN/MCN); serous cysts are 'serene' (benign).

items.label_md: Molecular subtypes of pancreatic cancer (Collisson, Moffitt, Bailey)
items.gloss_md: Transcriptomic classifications of PDAC that converge on two main tumour-intrinsic programmes, classical (pancreatic progenitor) and basal-like (squamous, quasi-mesenchymal).
items.body_md:
- Collisson et al. (Nature Medicine 2011): classical, quasi-mesenchymal (QM-PDA, worst prognosis) and exocrine-like (later attributed largely to normal acinar contamination).
- Moffitt et al. (Nature Genetics 2015): virtual microdissection by non-negative matrix factorisation separated tumour subtypes (classical vs basal-like) from stromal subtypes (normal vs activated stroma).
- Bailey et al. (Nature 2016, ICGC): squamous, pancreatic progenitor, immunogenic and ADEX (aberrantly differentiated endocrine exocrine); immunogenic and ADEX largely reflect non-tumour cells.
- Puleo et al. (2018) combined tumour and microenvironment features into five subtypes; Chan-Seng-Yue et al. (Nature Genetics 2020) refined into classical-A/B, basal-like-A/B and hybrid states.

Consensus: squamous ≈ basal-like ≈ quasi-mesenchymal; pancreatic progenitor ≈ classical. Single-cell and spatial studies show both programmes coexist within tumours. Subtyping is not yet routine, but GATA6 (classical marker) and classifiers such as PurIST are being evaluated to guide chemotherapy choice.

attrs.mnemonic: Two flavours, many names: classical = progenitor; basal-like = squamous = quasi-mesenchymal.

items.gloss_md: The two main tumour-intrinsic transcriptional subtypes of PDAC: classical (better prognosis, more chemosensitive) and basal-like (worse prognosis, resistant to FOLFIRINOX).
items.body_md:
- Classical: epithelial, pancreatic-lineage transcription factors (GATA6, HNF1A, HNF4A, FOXA), mucins (*TFF1*, *CLDN18*); more common in resectable and early disease.
- Basal-like: squamous/basal keratins (*KRT5*, *KRT6A*, *KRT17*, *S100A2*), loss of endodermal identity (low GATA6), *TP63* programmes; enriched in metastatic disease and associated with *KRAS* allelic imbalance/amplification (Chan-Seng-Yue 2020).
- Prognosis: basal-like has shorter OS in resected and advanced disease.
- Prediction: in the COMPASS trial (Aung et al., Clin Cancer Res 2018), basal-like tumours rarely responded to mFOLFIRINOX; some data suggest relatively better results with gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel, which prospective trials (e.g. PASS-01) examined.
- Assays: RNA-seq classifiers (PurIST, single-sample), GATA6 RNA in situ hybridisation or IHC as surrogates.

The subtypes are plastic: tumour cells can shift states under therapy or microenvironmental signals (e.g. TGF-β, hypoxia, *KRAS* inhibition).

attrs.mnemonic: Classical = 'classy' (better behaved, GATA6 high); basal-like = 'bad' (squamous-like, poor prognosis).

items.gloss_md: The dense fibro-inflammatory stroma (desmoplasia) that makes up most of the volume of a PDAC and shapes its biology, immunity and drug delivery.
items.body_md:
- Stroma can constitute up to about 80–90% of tumour volume; consists of CAFs (largely from activated pancreatic stellate cells), collagen, hyaluronan, immune cells, few and compressed blood vessels, and nerves.
- Effects: hypovascularity and high interstitial pressure (poor drug delivery), hypoxia and nutrient deprivation, T-cell exclusion, growth-factor and cytokine signalling (TGF-β, IL-6, Hedgehog), perineural invasion.
- Pancreatic stellate cells: quiescent, vitamin A–storing cells that become α-SMA⁺ myofibroblasts upon injury (similar to hepatic stellate cells in liver fibrosis).
- Therapeutic attempts: Hedgehog inhibition (IPI-926/saridegib improved drug delivery in KPC mice, Olive et al. 2009, but failed clinically), PEGPH20 to degrade hyaluronan (failed in phase III HALO-301), FAK inhibitors, vitamin D receptor ligands to reprogram stellate cells, CAF subtype targeting.
- Paradox: depleting stroma in mouse models accelerated tumours, so modern strategies aim at reprogramming rather than ablating it.

attrs.mnemonic: PDAC is 'more scar than cancer': up to nine parts stroma to one part tumour cells.

items.gloss_md: PDAC has a highly immunosuppressive, T-cell-poor microenvironment dominated by myeloid cells, making it a prototypical cold tumour.
items.body_md:
- Composition: abundant TAMs, MDSCs and neutrophils, regulatory T cells, few and dysfunctional CD8 T cells, mostly confined to stroma (immune-excluded); tertiary lymphoid structures in a minority.
- Drivers: oncogenic *KRAS* (GM-CSF, CXCL1, IL-6), CAF-derived TGF-β and CXCL12, low TMB and few neoantigens, low MHC class I (autophagy-mediated degradation shown by Yamamoto et al., Nature 2020).
- Clinical consequence: checkpoint inhibitors alone or in combination (anti-PD-1 + anti-CTLA-4) have shown little activity outside MSI-H/dMMR tumours.
- Strategies under investigation: CD40 agonists (to activate macrophages and dendritic cells), CXCR4 or CCR2 blockade, focal adhesion kinase inhibitors, neoantigen vaccines, KRAS-targeted T-cell therapies, combinations with KRAS inhibitors (which can increase T-cell infiltration in mouse models).

Long-term survivors show stronger neoantigen-specific CD8 responses, proving that effective immunity against PDAC is possible.

items.gloss_md: PDAC arising in carriers of germline cancer-predisposition variants or in families with clustering of pancreatic cancer.
items.body_md:
- About 5–10% of PDAC patients carry a germline pathogenic variant, often without a suggestive family history; hence guidelines (e.g. NCCN, ASCO) recommend germline testing for all patients with PDAC.
- Genes: *BRCA2* (most frequent), *BRCA1*, *PALB2*, *ATM*, *CDKN2A* (FAMMM, melanoma–pancreatic cancer syndrome), *STK11* (Peutz–Jeghers, very high risk), mismatch-repair genes (Lynch), *PRSS1*/*SPINK1*/*CFTR* (hereditary and chronic pancreatitis), *TP53*.
- Familial pancreatic cancer (FPC): at least two first-degree relatives with PDAC without a known syndrome; risk rises with the number of affected relatives. In Germany, the FaPaCa registry (Marburg) collects such families.
- Therapeutic consequences: platinum-based chemotherapy and olaparib maintenance (g*BRCA*), checkpoint inhibitors (Lynch/dMMR).
- Family consequences: cascade testing and surveillance of high-risk relatives.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Test everyone': every PDAC patient gets germline testing, family history or not.

items.label_md: Surveillance of high-risk individuals for pancreatic cancer
items.gloss_md: Regular imaging (EUS and/or MRI) of people with a strongly increased lifetime risk of PDAC to detect early cancers and high-grade precursors.
items.body_md:
The International Cancer of the Pancreas Screening (CAPS) Consortium (Goggins et al., Gut 2020) recommends surveillance for:
- People with ≥2 affected relatives with PDAC, at least one first-degree (familial pancreatic cancer).
- Carriers of *STK11* (Peutz–Jeghers) and *CDKN2A* variants regardless of family history.
- Carriers of *BRCA2*, *BRCA1*, *PALB2*, *ATM* or mismatch-repair variants with at least one affected first-degree relative.
- Hereditary pancreatitis (*PRSS1*).

Start ages are typically 50 (or 40 for *CDKN2A*/*STK11*, 10 years before the youngest affected relative), with annual MRI/MRCP and/or EUS and glucose/HbA1c. Surveillance downstages detected cancers in cohort studies, but overtreatment of benign lesions and costs are concerns; it should be done in expert centres or trials.

items.gloss_md: The roughly 8–10% of PDACs without a *KRAS* mutation, which are enriched for alternative, often targetable MAPK-activating drivers.
items.body_md:
Typical alterations:
- Gene fusions: *NRG1* (zenocutuzumab, an anti-HER2/HER3 bispecific antibody, approved by the FDA in 2024 for *NRG1*-fusion NSCLC and pancreatic cancer), *NTRK1-3* (larotrectinib, entrectinib), *ALK*, *ROS1*, *RET* (selpercatinib), *FGFR2*, *BRAF* fusions.
- *BRAF* V600E or in-frame deletions (dabrafenib/trametinib for V600E).
- Mismatch-repair deficiency (checkpoint inhibitors).
- *ERBB2* amplification, *GNAS*-driven tumours.

Such tumours occur more often in younger patients. Germline variants and acinar cell carcinoma (a different entity, often *KRAS*-wild-type with *BRAF* fusions) should be excluded. Comprehensive DNA- and RNA-based profiling (RNA for fusions) is recommended for *KRAS*-wild-type PDAC. The BxPC-3 cell line is a *KRAS*-wild-type PDAC model.

items.gloss_md: Reprogramming of pancreatic acinar cells into duct-like cells in response to injury or inflammation, which, combined with oncogenic *KRAS*, can give rise to PanIN.
items.body_md:
- Triggers: pancreatitis, inflammatory cytokines, EGFR signalling.
- Normally reversible; persistent *KRAS* activation locks cells in the ductal state and drives PanIN formation.
- Mouse lineage tracing showed that acinar cells (and less readily duct cells) can be the cell of origin of PanIN and PDAC; pancreatitis strongly accelerates tumourigenesis in Kras-mutant mice (Guerra et al. 2007).
- Molecular players: SOX9 (ductal), loss of acinar transcription factors PTF1A, MIST1 (BHLHA15), NR5A2; chromatin and epigenetic changes.

ADM links the clinical risk factor chronic pancreatitis to PDAC development.

items.gloss_md: The standard genetically engineered mouse model of PDAC carrying pancreas-specific *Kras* G12D and mutant *Trp53* R172H.
items.body_md:
- Genotype: LSL-Kras^G12D/+; LSL-Trp53^R172H/+; Pdx1-Cre (Hingorani et al., Cancer Cell 2005). Cre recombinase expressed from the Pdx1 promoter removes the lox-stop-lox cassettes in the pancreatic lineage.
- KC model (LSL-Kras^G12D; Pdx1-Cre or Ptf1a-Cre; Hingorani 2003): develops PanINs and, slowly, invasive cancer.
- KPC mice develop invasive, metastatic PDAC with desmoplastic stroma within months, closely mimicking human histology, immune suppression and drug resistance.
- Uses: preclinical therapy trials (e.g. the Hedgehog inhibitor study, Olive 2009), stroma and immunology research; syngeneic KPC cell lines for orthotopic transplantation into immunocompetent mice.
- Variants: KPPC (homozygous p53 loss), Ptf1a-Cre-based models, inducible and dual-recombinase systems.

attrs.mnemonic: K-P-C = Kras, P53, Cre.

items.gloss_md: Subtypes of pancreatic ductal carcinoma recognised by the WHO that differ in morphology, genetics and prognosis from conventional tubular PDAC.
items.body_md:
- Adenosquamous carcinoma: ≥30% squamous component; aggressive.
- Colloid (mucinous non-cystic) carcinoma: abundant extracellular mucin; usually arises from intestinal-type IPMN; considerably better prognosis.
- Medullary carcinoma: syncytial growth, pushing borders, lymphocytes; associated with MSI and Lynch syndrome.
- Undifferentiated carcinoma (anaplastic, sarcomatoid) and undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells.
- Signet-ring cell carcinoma, hepatoid carcinoma, invasive micropapillary carcinoma.

Distinct pancreatic malignancies that are not PDAC: acinar cell carcinoma (enzyme production, sometimes lipase hypersecretion with fat necrosis), pancreatoblastoma (children), solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, neuroendocrine neoplasms. Recognising variants matters for prognosis and for molecular testing (e.g. MMR in medullary carcinoma).

items.gloss_md: Infiltration of tumour cells into and along nerves, found in the large majority of resected PDACs and linked to pain and local recurrence.
items.body_md:
- Recorded as Pn1 in the TNM tumour formula.
- PDAC spreads along the nerve plexuses around the SMA and coeliac axis (extrapancreatic plexus invasion), a reason for R1 resections at the SMA margin and for local recurrence.
- Mechanisms: neurotrophic factors (NGF, GDNF, artemin), chemokines (CXCL12/CX3CL1), Schwann cells guiding tumour cells; nerves in turn release neurotransmitters that promote tumour growth (cancer neuroscience).
- Clinical: neural invasion causes the typical back pain; coeliac plexus neurolysis targets it.
- Prognosis: extensive or extrapancreatic neural invasion is associated with shorter survival.

items.gloss_md: A four-drug chemotherapy regimen of 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan and oxaliplatin, the most active standard regimen for fit patients with pancreatic cancer.
items.body_md:
- Components (every 14 days): oxaliplatin 85 mg/m², irinotecan 180 mg/m², leucovorin 400 mg/m², 5-FU 400 mg/m² bolus followed by 2400 mg/m² as a 46-hour infusion.
- ACCORD 11/PRODIGE 4 (Conroy et al., NEJM 2011): metastatic PDAC, ECOG 0–1, age ≤75, normal-ish bilirubin; median OS 11.1 vs 6.8 months with gemcitabine; ORR about 32% vs 9%; more toxicity (neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, diarrhoea, neuropathy) but slower decline in quality of life.
- Used across settings: metastatic first-line, induction in locally advanced disease, neoadjuvant in borderline-resectable disease, and (as modified FOLFIRINOX) adjuvant after resection.
- Requirements: good performance status, adequate organ function, bilirubin near normal (biliary stent if needed), *DPYD* testing; G-CSF prophylaxis often used.

In practice most centres use modified FOLFIRINOX (no 5-FU bolus, reduced irinotecan).

attrs.mnemonic: FOL-F-IRI-N-OX = FOLinic acid + Fluorouracil + IRInotecan + OXaliplatin: the name lists all four drugs.
attrs.anecdote: FOLFIRINOX was developed by Thierry Conroy's French PRODIGE group; the 2011 NEJM paper ended 14 years in which gemcitabine monotherapy had been the unchallenged standard for metastatic pancreatic cancer.

items.gloss_md: A dose-modified, better-tolerated FOLFIRINOX without the 5-FU bolus and with irinotecan reduced to 150 mg/m², the standard adjuvant regimen for fit patients after PDAC resection.
items.body_md:
- Usual modifications (as in PRODIGE 24): no 5-FU bolus, irinotecan 150 mg/m² instead of 180 mg/m²; oxaliplatin 85 mg/m², leucovorin 400 mg/m², 5-FU 2400 mg/m² over 46 h, every 14 days.
- Adjuvant (PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6, Conroy et al., NEJM 2018): 12 cycles (6 months) after R0/R1 resection; median DFS 21.6 vs 12.8 months and median OS 54.4 vs 35.0 months compared with gemcitabine. Eligibility: ECOG 0–1, age 18–79, CA19-9 <180 U/mL postoperatively, start within 12 weeks.
- Neoadjuvant and metastatic settings: widely used instead of full-dose FOLFIRINOX, with retrospective data suggesting similar efficacy and less toxicity.
- Toxicities: diarrhoea, neutropenia, fatigue, neuropathy (oxaliplatin; often stopped first).

attrs.mnemonic: 'm' = minus: minus the bolus, minus 30 mg/m² irinotecan (180 → 150).

items.gloss_md: A first-line combination for metastatic pancreatic cancer (MPACT trial), less toxic than FOLFIRINOX and suitable for patients with somewhat lower performance status.
items.body_md:
- Schedule: nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m² followed by gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² on days 1, 8 and 15 every 28 days.
- MPACT (Von Hoff et al., NEJM 2013): 861 patients with metastatic PDAC, KPS ≥70; median OS 8.5 vs 6.7 months with gemcitabine alone (HR 0.72); ORR 23% vs 7%.
- Toxicities: neutropenia, fatigue, peripheral neuropathy (usually reversible after dose reduction), alopecia.
- Other uses: neoadjuvant or induction therapy (e.g. LAPC), second-line after FOLFIRINOX; in the adjuvant APACT trial it did not meet its primary endpoint, so it is not standard adjuvant therapy.
- Choice vs FOLFIRINOX: no head-to-head phase III trial; FOLFIRINOX/NALIRIFOX for the fittest patients, gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel when ECOG is 1–2, in older patients or with comorbidities. In NAPOLI-3, NALIRIFOX was superior to this combination.

German shorthand: "Gem/nab-P" or "Gem/Abraxane".

attrs.mnemonic: MPACT = 'eMPACT': 8.5 vs 6.7 months — roughly two extra months over gemcitabine alone.

items.gloss_md: A first-line regimen for metastatic PDAC combining liposomal irinotecan, oxaliplatin, 5-FU and leucovorin, superior to gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel in the NAPOLI-3 trial.
items.body_md:
- Components (every 14 days): liposomal irinotecan 50 mg/m², oxaliplatin 60 mg/m², leucovorin 400 mg/m², 5-FU 2400 mg/m² over 46 h.
- NAPOLI-3 (Wainberg et al., Lancet 2023): 770 patients; median OS 11.1 vs 9.2 months (HR 0.83) and PFS 7.4 vs 5.6 months vs gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel.
- FDA approval in February 2024 for first-line metastatic PDAC.
- It has never been compared directly with (m)FOLFIRINOX; efficacy appears similar across trials, and liposomal irinotecan is considerably more expensive, so its role relative to FOLFIRINOX is debated.
- Toxicity: diarrhoea, nausea, hypokalaemia, neutropenia; less neuropathy because of the lower oxaliplatin dose.

attrs.mnemonic: NAL-IRI-FOX = NAnoLiposomal IRInotecan + FOX (Fluorouracil, OXaliplatin) — FOLFIRINOX with a liposomal coat.

items.gloss_md: An adjuvant regimen for resected PDAC (ESPAC-4) used for patients not fit enough for mFOLFIRINOX.
items.body_md:
- Schedule: gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² days 1, 8, 15 every 28 days plus oral capecitabine 1660 mg/m²/day for 21 of 28 days, for 6 cycles.
- ESPAC-4 (Neoptolemos et al., Lancet 2017): median OS 28.0 vs 25.5 months compared with gemcitabine alone (HR 0.82); later analyses showed a larger 5-year survival difference.
- Position: second choice in adjuvant therapy after mFOLFIRINOX (for ECOG 2, age, comorbidities); gemcitabine alone if GemCap is not tolerated.
- Also used in the metastatic setting for frail patients.

items.label_md: Adjuvant chemotherapy for resected pancreatic cancer
items.gloss_md: Six months of chemotherapy after PDAC resection, the standard of care that roughly doubles long-term survival compared with surgery alone.
items.body_md:
Evidence history:
- ESPAC-1 (2004): adjuvant 5-FU/LV improved survival; chemoradiation did not.
- CONKO-001 (Oettle et al., JAMA 2007 and 2013, German trial): gemcitabine vs observation improved DFS and OS (5-year OS about 21% vs 10%).
- ESPAC-3 (2010): gemcitabine and 5-FU/LV equivalent.
- ESPAC-4 (2017): gemcitabine + capecitabine superior to gemcitabine (median OS 28.0 vs 25.5 months).
- PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6 (2018): mFOLFIRINOX superior to gemcitabine (median OS 54.4 vs 35.0 months).
- APACT (2022): gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel did not meet its primary endpoint.

Current recommendation: mFOLFIRINOX for fit patients (ECOG 0–1), otherwise gemcitabine/capecitabine or gemcitabine monotherapy; start within about 12 weeks after surgery; patients after neoadjuvant therapy often receive the remainder of a 6-month total course. Around a quarter to a half of patients never start adjuvant therapy because of postoperative complications, one argument for neoadjuvant approaches. Japan uses S-1 (JASPAC 01).

attrs.mnemonic: Adjuvant ladder by fitness: mFOLFIRINOX → GemCap → Gem; always 6 months.
attrs.anecdote: CONKO-001 was a German multicentre trial led from the Charité in Berlin; it established gemcitabine as adjuvant standard and was one of the few PDAC trials with a meaningful 10-year survival readout.

items.gloss_md: Chemotherapy (± radiotherapy) before resection of PDAC; standard for borderline-resectable disease and increasingly used, but still debated, for resectable disease.
items.body_md:
Rationale: PDAC is systemic early (most resected patients relapse), many patients never receive adjuvant therapy after a Whipple, and progression during neoadjuvant therapy identifies patients who would not benefit from surgery.

- Borderline resectable: neoadjuvant (m)FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel (± chemoradiation) is the recommended standard in NCCN, ESMO and German S3 guidelines.
- Resectable: upfront surgery followed by adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX remains standard in many guidelines; NCCN suggests neoadjuvant therapy for high-risk features (very high CA19-9, large tumours or nodes, severe weight loss or pain). Trials: PREOPANC (gemcitabine-based chemoradiation, long-term OS benefit), NORPACT-1 (neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX, no OS benefit), and further ongoing trials (e.g. Alliance A021806, PREOPANC-3).
- Restaging: CT rarely shows shrinkage; CA19-9 response, stable/improved performance status and absence of metastasis justify exploration.
- Pathology: ypTNM, tumour regression grade; major pathological response predicts better survival.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Test the biology before the knife': neoadjuvant therapy lets the aggressive tumours declare themselves before a big operation.

items.label_md: Second-line therapy for metastatic pancreatic cancer
items.gloss_md: Treatment after progression on first-line chemotherapy, usually switching between fluoropyrimidine- and gemcitabine-based regimens.
items.body_md:
- After gemcitabine-based first line: liposomal irinotecan + 5-FU/LV (NAPOLI-1, Wang-Gillam et al., Lancet 2016: median OS 6.1 vs 4.2 months vs 5-FU/LV), FOLFOX or OFF (oxaliplatin, 5-FU, folinic acid; German CONKO-003 positive, Canadian PANCREOX negative), or FOLFIRINOX in fit patients.
- After FOLFIRINOX: gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel or gemcitabine alone (supported by retrospective and phase II data).
- Biomarker-driven: *KRAS* G12C inhibitors, NTRK/RET/NRG1-targeted drugs, checkpoint inhibitors for dMMR; clinical trials (e.g. RAS(ON) inhibitors).
- About half of patients are fit enough for second-line therapy; best supportive care is the alternative.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Swap the backbone': Gem first → 5-FU next, 5-FU first → Gem next.

items.label_md: Olaparib maintenance in germline BRCA-mutated pancreatic cancer (POLO)
items.gloss_md: Maintenance therapy with the PARP inhibitor olaparib for metastatic PDAC with a germline *BRCA1/2* mutation whose disease has not progressed on at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum-based chemotherapy.
items.body_md:
- POLO trial (Golan et al., NEJM 2019): 154 patients randomised 3:2 to olaparib 300 mg twice daily or placebo; median PFS 7.4 vs 3.8 months (HR 0.53). Final OS analysis (Kindler et al., JCO 2022): 19.0 vs 19.2 months, no significant difference; a subset had long-lasting benefit.
- Approved by FDA (2019) and EMA (2020) for this indication.
- About 4–7% of PDAC patients have a germline *BRCA1/2* variant, which is one reason for universal germline testing.
- Practical sequence: platinum induction (e.g. FOLFIRINOX) for ≥16 weeks → olaparib maintenance (chemotherapy-free interval with good quality of life).
- Somatic *BRCA* or *PALB2* alterations: supported by phase II data (rucaparib), not by POLO.

attrs.mnemonic: POLO = Pancreas Cancer OLaparib Ongoing; rule '16 weeks platinum, then PARP'.

items.gloss_md: Small molecules that directly inhibit mutant KRAS (allele-specific, e.g. G12C or G12D) or multiple RAS proteins (pan-RAS, RAS(ON) inhibitors), a new therapeutic class with high relevance for PDAC.
items.body_md:
- G12C (OFF-state, covalent): sotorasib (first approved 2021 for NSCLC) and adagrasib; in PDAC G12C occurs in only about 1–2%; sotorasib showed an ORR of 21% in CodeBreaK 100 (Strickler et al., NEJM 2023), adagrasib similar activity in KRYSTAL-1; guidelines list them as options for *KRAS* G12C PDAC.
- G12D-selective inhibitors (G12D is the most common PDAC allele): e.g. MRTX1133 (non-covalent) and zoldonrasib (RMC-9805, covalent RAS(ON)), in early trials.
- RAS(ON) multi-selective inhibitors: daraxonrasib (RMC-6236), a tri-complex inhibitor that binds active GTP-bound RAS together with cyclophilin A; promising early PDAC data led to the phase III RASolute 302 trial in previously treated metastatic PDAC.
- Pan-KRAS inhibitors (sparing HRAS/NRAS) and degraders are in development.
- Resistance: secondary *KRAS* mutations or amplification, other RTK/RAS/MAPK alterations, *MYC*, YAP/TAZ activation, epithelial-to-mesenchymal and lineage switching.

For decades KRAS was called "undruggable" because its smooth surface and picomolar GTP affinity offered no pocket; combinations with chemotherapy and immunotherapy are under study.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Undruggable no more': G12C first (cysteine to grab), then G12D, then all RAS in the ON state.
attrs.anecdote: Kevan Shokat's lab discovered the switch-II pocket of KRAS G12C in 2013 (Ostrem et al., Nature), and covalent drugs targeting the mutant cysteine reached approval only eight years later — after almost 40 years of failed attempts to drug KRAS.

items.gloss_md: People with the Lewis (a−b−) blood-group phenotype lack fucosyltransferase 3 activity and cannot produce CA19-9, so their marker stays low even with advanced pancreatic cancer.
items.body_md:
- CA19-9 is sialyl-Lewis-a; its synthesis requires the Lewis enzyme FUT3. About 5–10% of people (varying by ancestry) are Lewis-negative.
- Consequence: a normal or undetectable CA19-9 (often <2 U/mL) cannot be used to exclude or monitor PDAC in these patients.
- Clues: CA19-9 near zero despite a large tumour; Lewis typing can be done serologically or genetically.
- Alternatives for monitoring: CEA, CA-125, DUPAN-2 (used in Japan), imaging, ctDNA.
- Some data suggest Lewis-negative patients have a different (possibly worse) prognosis, but evidence is inconsistent.

When reading trials, remember that CA19-9-based inclusion criteria or response definitions do not apply to these "non-secretors" of CA19-9.

attrs.mnemonic: No Lewis, no CA19-9: the marker is a Lewis antigen, so without Lewis the tumour stays 'silent' in the blood.

items.label_md: New-onset diabetes as an early sign of pancreatic cancer
items.gloss_md: Diabetes appearing for the first time in a person over about 50 years can be an early manifestation of an undiagnosed PDAC (paraneoplastic or due to gland destruction).
items.body_md:
- About 1% of people over 50 with new-onset diabetes are diagnosed with pancreatic cancer within 3 years (Chari et al., Gastroenterology 2005), roughly eight times the general population rate.
- Mechanism: tumour-derived factors cause insulin resistance and β-cell dysfunction (paraneoplastic), plus destruction of islets; diabetes may improve after resection.
- Warning signs: weight loss with new hyperglycaemia (in type 2 diabetes, weight usually increases beforehand).
- Risk model: ENDPAC score (age at onset, weight change, glucose change) to select patients for imaging; prospective studies are ongoing.
- Distinguish from long-standing type 2 diabetes (moderate risk factor) and type 3c diabetes after pancreatic disease.

The Kyoto IPMN guidelines added new-onset or worsening diabetes as a worrisome feature.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Sweet and slim is suspicious': new diabetes with weight loss over 50.

items.gloss_md: Diabetes caused by disease of the exocrine pancreas (pancreatitis, cancer, resection, cystic fibrosis), with loss of both insulin and glucagon secretion.
items.body_md:
- Causes: chronic pancreatitis (most common), PDAC, pancreatic resection (especially total and distal pancreatectomy), cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis.
- Features: insulin deficiency plus loss of glucagon and pancreatic polypeptide → glucose variability and hypoglycaemia risk ("brittle" diabetes, most extreme after total pancreatectomy); usually coexists with exocrine insufficiency.
- Frequently misclassified as type 2 diabetes.
- Management: metformin early, insulin often needed; continuous glucose monitoring; treat exocrine insufficiency (malabsorption worsens glycaemic control).

After Whipple, new diabetes develops in a minority; after distal pancreatectomy more often (more islet mass in the tail).

attrs.mnemonic: Type 3c — 'c' for 'cut out or chewed up' pancreas (resection, pancreatitis, cancer).

items.gloss_md: Inadequate secretion of pancreatic digestive enzymes, causing maldigestion of fat and protein, steatorrhoea and weight loss; very common in PDAC and after pancreatic surgery.
items.body_md:
- Causes in oncology: tumour obstruction of the pancreatic duct (head tumours), loss of parenchyma, resection (nearly universal after Whipple and total pancreatectomy), plus asynchrony of food and enzymes after reconstruction.
- Symptoms: steatorrhoea (fatty, foul-smelling stools), bloating, flatulence, weight loss, deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
- Diagnosis: faecal elastase-1 <200 µg/g (severe <100 µg/g); not reliable with watery stools; often treated empirically after resection.
- Treatment: pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) with pancrelipase/pancreatin capsules (e.g. Kreon), taken with meals; typical starting dose about 40,000–50,000 lipase units per main meal and half with snacks; titrate to symptoms; add proton-pump inhibitor if response is insufficient.

PERT is underprescribed; treating EPI improves nutrition and is associated with better survival in PDAC.

attrs.mnemonic: 'Elastase below 200 = enzymes needed': give lipase with every meal, no meal without Kreon.

items.gloss_md: A multifactorial syndrome of ongoing skeletal muscle loss (with or without fat loss) that cannot be fully reversed by nutrition, present in most patients with advanced PDAC.
items.body_md:
- International consensus definition (Fearon et al., Lancet Oncology 2011): weight loss >5% in 6 months, or BMI <20 kg/m² with weight loss >2%, or sarcopenia with weight loss >2%. Stages: pre-cachexia, cachexia, refractory cachexia.
- Frequency: PDAC has one of the highest cachexia rates of all cancers (most patients at diagnosis have lost weight).
- Mechanisms: systemic inflammation (IL-6, TNF), tumour-derived factors (GDF15, activin), anorexia, exocrine insufficiency, altered adipose and muscle metabolism.
- Measurement: weight history, CT-based body composition (skeletal muscle index at L3), grip strength.
- Management: multimodal — nutritional counselling and supplements, PERT, exercise, treating symptoms; anamorelin (ghrelin agonist, approved in Japan); anti-GDF15 antibody ponsegromab improved weight in a phase II trial (NEJM 2024).

Cachexia reduces chemotherapy tolerance and survival.

attrs.mnemonic: Fearon's '5–2–2': >5% loss, or >2% with BMI <20, or >2% with sarcopenia.

items.gloss_md: Pancreatic cancer carries one of the highest risks of venous thromboembolism among all cancers, relevant for prophylaxis and treatment decisions.
items.body_md:
- Khorana score (risk of chemotherapy-associated VTE): very-high-risk site (stomach, pancreas) 2 points; high-risk site (lung, lymphoma, gynaecological, bladder, testicular) 1; platelets ≥350,000/µL 1; haemoglobin <10 g/dL or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents 1; leukocytes >11,000/µL 1; BMI ≥35 kg/m² 1. Score ≥2 is high risk; every PDAC patient starts at 2.
- Primary prophylaxis: low-molecular-weight heparin or direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban in AVERT, rivaroxaban in CASSINI) can be considered for ambulatory high-risk patients on chemotherapy, weighing bleeding risk.
- Treatment of cancer-associated VTE: LMWH or DOACs (apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban), with caution for GI and urothelial tumours because of bleeding.
- Also: portal/splenic/mesenteric vein thrombosis from tumour invasion, and Trousseau syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis).

attrs.mnemonic: Pancreas = 2 points in Khorana by itself: every PDAC patient starts 'high risk'.

items.gloss_md: Treatment of the often severe visceral and neuropathic pain of PDAC with analgesics, coeliac plexus neurolysis and radiotherapy.
items.body_md:
- Cause: infiltration of the coeliac and mesenteric nerve plexuses (perineural invasion), ductal obstruction, organ distension; typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, worse lying flat.
- Analgesics: WHO stepwise approach — non-opioids (metamizole is common in Germany, paracetamol), opioids (morphine, hydromorphone, oxycodone, fentanyl patches), co-analgesics for neuropathic pain (gabapentinoids, antidepressants); laxatives with opioids.
- Coeliac plexus neurolysis: injection of alcohol around the coeliac ganglia, usually EUS-guided (or percutaneous/intraoperative); reduces pain and opioid consumption for weeks to months.
- Palliative radiotherapy or SBRT for local pain.
- Treating exocrine insufficiency and obstruction (stents) addresses non-neural pain.

Early palliative-care involvement improves symptom control.

items.label_md: Biliary tract cancer: oncological management and molecular targets
items.gloss_md: The oncological view of cholangiocarcinoma (intrahepatic, perihilar, distal) and gallbladder cancer: staging-relevant subtypes, systemic therapy and targetable alterations.
items.body_md:
- Subtypes: intrahepatic (iCCA, mass in the liver), perihilar (pCCA, Klatskin tumour at the hepatic duct bifurcation; Bismuth–Corlette types I–IV), distal (dCCA, in the pancreatic head region, resected by Whipple).
- Risk factors: primary sclerosing cholangitis (often with ulcerative colitis), liver flukes (*Opisthorchis*, *Clonorchis*; very common in Southeast Asia), choledochal cysts, hepatolithiasis, cirrhosis, chronic HBV/HCV, MASLD.
- Diagnosis: MRI/MRCP, CT, ERCP brushing/cholangioscopy, CA19-9; iCCA must be distinguished from HCC and from metastases of other adenocarcinomas.
- Treatment: resection (often major liver resection) + adjuvant capecitabine (BILCAP); liver transplantation for selected unresectable pCCA after neoadjuvant chemoradiation (Mayo protocol); first-line gemcitabine/cisplatin + durvalumab (TOPAZ-1) or pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-966).
- Molecular targets (mostly iCCA): *FGFR2* fusions (pemigatinib, futibatinib), *IDH1* mutations (ivosidenib), HER2 amplification (zanidatamab, mostly gallbladder/extrahepatic), *BRAF* V600E, *NTRK*, MSI-H — molecular profiling is standard in advanced disease.

German: Cholangiozelluläres Karzinom (CCC), Gallengangskarzinom.

attrs.mnemonic: In German clinics 'CCC' can mean cholangiocellular carcinoma or Comprehensive Cancer Center — context decides.

items.gloss_md: Cancers arising at or near the ampulla of Vater (ampulla, distal bile duct, duodenum, pancreatic head) that present with jaundice and are treated by pancreatoduodenectomy.
items.body_md:
- Periampullary cancers: pancreatic head PDAC (most common), distal cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary carcinoma, duodenal adenocarcinoma.
- Ampullary carcinoma subtypes: intestinal (better prognosis, CK20⁺/CDX2⁺, treated more like colorectal cancer) and pancreatobiliary (worse, CK7⁺/MUC1⁺, treated more like PDAC); mixed forms exist.
- Present early with jaundice, so more often resectable and with better prognosis than PDAC.
- Familial adenomatous polyposis carries a high risk of duodenal and ampullary adenomas.
- Higher postoperative fistula risk than PDAC because the pancreas is usually soft with a narrow duct.

Pathologists must determine the epicentre of the tumour to assign the origin, which affects staging (separate TNM chapters) and adjuvant therapy.

items.gloss_md: Adenocarcinoma of the colon or rectum, one of the most common cancers, arising mostly from adenomas via the adenoma–carcinoma sequence.
items.body_md:
- Epidemiology: among the three most common cancers in Germany; screening by colonoscopy (removal of adenomas) or faecal immunochemical test (FIT) reduces incidence and mortality.
- Pathways: chromosomal instability (~85%; *APC*, *KRAS*, *TP53*, *SMAD4*), MSI/dMMR (~15%; Lynch or sporadic *MLH1* methylation), serrated pathway (*BRAF* V600E, CpG island methylator phenotype).
- Stage-based treatment: colon stage III → adjuvant FOLFOX or CAPOX (3 months CAPOX sufficient for low-risk stage III, IDEA collaboration); rectal cancer → neoadjuvant (chemo)radiotherapy or total neoadjuvant therapy, possibly "watch and wait" after complete response; dMMR rectal cancer can respond completely to PD-1 blockade alone (dostarlimab).
- Metastatic: mandatory testing for *RAS*, *BRAF*, MSI and HER2; FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR (only *RAS* wild-type, mainly left-sided primaries) or bevacizumab; pembrolizumab first-line for MSI-H (KEYNOTE-177); encorafenib + cetuximab for *BRAF* V600E; resection of liver metastases can be curative.
- Marker: CEA for follow-up.

attrs.mnemonic: Left-sided RAS wild-type = 'EGFR territory'; right-sided tumours behave differently (more MSI, BRAF, worse response to anti-EGFR).
attrs.anecdote: In 2022 Cercek et al. (NEJM) reported that all 12 patients with dMMR rectal cancer treated with dostarlimab alone had a complete clinical response, avoiding surgery and radiotherapy — an unprecedented result.

items.label_md: Consensus molecular subtypes of colorectal cancer (CMS)
items.gloss_md: A transcriptome-based classification of colorectal cancer into four subtypes (CMS1–4) agreed by an international consortium.
items.body_md:
Guinney et al., Nature Medicine 2015:
- CMS1 (MSI immune, ~14%): hypermutated, MSI, *BRAF* V600E, strong immune infiltration; poor survival after relapse.
- CMS2 (canonical, ~37%): epithelial, WNT and MYC activation, chromosomal instability.
- CMS3 (metabolic, ~13%): metabolic dysregulation, frequent *KRAS* mutations.
- CMS4 (mesenchymal, ~23%): TGF-β activation, stromal invasion, angiogenesis; worst relapse-free and overall survival.
- Remaining ~13% mixed or unclassified.

Like PDAC subtypes, CMS4 is strongly driven by stromal content, so tumour-intrinsic classifiers (CRIS, iCMS) were developed later. CMS is used in research and trial stratification but not yet routinely in clinical decisions. It is a model example of consensus subtyping by integrating several classification systems.

items.gloss_md: A neoplasm of the pancreatic endocrine cells, usually a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour with far better prognosis than PDAC; can be hormone-producing (functional) or non-functional.
items.body_md:
- Frequency: a few percent of pancreatic neoplasms; increasingly detected incidentally.
- Functional: insulinoma (most common functional, mostly benign; Whipple's triad of hypoglycaemia), gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, often duodenal, MEN1), glucagonoma (necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes), VIPoma (watery diarrhoea), somatostatinoma. Non-functional tumours are the majority.
- Grading: WHO NET G1/G2/G3 by Ki-67 (<3%, 3–20%, >20%) vs poorly differentiated NEC.
- Genetics: *MEN1*, *DAXX*/*ATRX* (alternative lengthening of telomeres) and mTOR-pathway genes (Jiao et al., Science 2011); syndromes MEN1, VHL, NF1, tuberous sclerosis.
- Imaging: somatostatin-receptor PET (⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE/DOTATOC), FDG-PET for higher grades; chromogranin A as a marker.
- Treatment: resection (small non-functional NETs <2 cm may be observed); somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide; CLARINET), everolimus, sunitinib, capecitabine/temozolomide (CAPTEM), peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE), liver-directed therapy; NEC: platinum/etoposide.
- Has its own TNM classification.

attrs.mnemonic: DAXX/ATRX, MEN1, mTOR — 'D-A-M': the three classic gene groups in PanNETs.
attrs.anecdote: Steve Jobs had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour (not PDAC), diagnosed in 2003; he delayed surgery for about nine months, later had a Whipple operation and a liver transplant, and died in 2011.

items.gloss_md: Cancers that occur more often in transplant recipients because long-term immunosuppression impairs tumour immunosurveillance and control of oncogenic viruses.
items.body_md:
- Overall cancer risk is roughly two- to fourfold higher than in the general population, with very different risks by type.
- Non-melanoma skin cancer, especially cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma: the most common malignancy, with a many-fold increased risk and aggressive course; the usual ratio of basal-cell to squamous-cell carcinoma is reversed.
- Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD): mostly EBV-driven B-cell lymphoma; highest risk in EBV-seronegative recipients of seropositive organs (children), in the first year and with T-cell-depleting induction; treatment: reduce immunosuppression, rituximab, chemotherapy, EBV-specific T cells (tabelecleucel).
- Virus-associated cancers: Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), HPV-related anogenital cancers, Merkel cell carcinoma.
- Others: renal cell carcinoma in native kidneys, recurrence of HCC after liver transplantation (selection by Milan criteria), donor-transmitted cancers.
- Prevention: lowest effective immunosuppression, switching calcineurin inhibitors to mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus) in patients with skin cancers, sun protection, regular dermatological and age-appropriate screening.
- Checkpoint inhibitors in transplant recipients carry a high risk of graft rejection.

attrs.mnemonic: Transplant cancers are 'skin, lymph and viruses': cSCC, PTLD (EBV), Kaposi (HHV-8), HPV.
